items.title: Pluto's long year
items.body: Pluto takes about 248 Earth years to go once around the Sun. Since its discovery in 1930, it has travelled less than half of one orbit.
items.hook: Wonder: where in the sky will Pluto be when it finally completes its first 'discovery year'?

items.title: Make 'I'm not sure' a valid answer
items.body: If your instructions only reward answers, an agent will produce answers. Tell it explicitly that 'I'm not sure, here's what I'd check' is acceptable. You'll get fewer confident guesses and more useful next steps.
items.q: What explicit permission reduces confident guessing from an agent?
items.a: Allowing it to say it isn't sure and suggest what to check.

items.title: Tea, second cup
items.body:
The first cup was for waking.
This one is for sitting
while the light walks slowly
across the floor
looking for nothing in particular.

items.title: Leko and Svidler will call the title match
items.body: GMs Peter Leko and Peter Svidler will commentate the 14-game World Championship match between Gukesh and Javokhir Sindarov, which begins on 24 November at the Fondation Martin Bodmer near Geneva.

items.title: What we may be
items.body: We know what we are, but know not what we may be.

items.title: Merkle trees: comparing big data cheaply
items.body: A Merkle tree hashes data in blocks, then hashes those hashes up to a single root. Two replicas can compare roots; if they match, everything matches. If not, they walk down only the branches that differ. Cassandra and Dynamo-style stores use this for quiet background repair.
items.hook: Wonder: how could two libraries check their catalogues match without reading every card?

items.title: Pineapples take their time
items.body: A pineapple plant usually needs around 18 to 24 months to produce a single fruit, and each plant gives just one main pineapple per cycle.
items.q: Roughly how long does a pineapple take to grow?
items.a: About 18 to 24 months.

items.title: The floppy began at eight inches
items.body: IBM's first floppy disk, introduced in 1971, was 8 inches across and read-only. It was made to load start-up instructions into mainframes. Smaller 5¼-inch and 3½-inch versions came later and carried software into homes.
items.hook: Wonder: what's the oldest storage medium you've ever held?

items.title: Old light from Andromeda
items.body: On a dark November evening, the Andromeda Galaxy appears as a faint smudge to the naked eye. Its light set out about 2.5 million years ago, so the glow you see left before our own species existed.
items.q: About how long has Andromeda's light been travelling to reach us?
items.a: About 2.5 million years.

items.title: Let the first try fail
items.body: When a character wants something, let their first attempt not quite work. The failure tells us what is in the way and makes the second attempt matter. Even in a 200-word story, one small stumble gives the ending somewhere to land.
items.hook: Wonder: what does your character try first, and why doesn't it work?

items.title: Reward now, not later
items.body: Rewards that arrive weeks later barely register for many ADHD brains; rewards that arrive right away do. Attach a small, immediate treat to the end of a dull task, such as a favourite song, a walk to the balcony or a cup of tea, so finishing pays off on the spot.

items.title: A statue measured in couplets
items.body: The Thiruvalluvar statue at Kanyakumari, unveiled on 1 January 2000, is 133 feet tall, one foot for each of the 133 chapters of the Thirukkural. It stands on a 38-foot pedestal that represents the 38 chapters on virtue.
items.q: Why is the Thiruvalluvar statue 133 feet tall?
items.a: One foot for each of the Thirukkural's 133 chapters.

items.title: How researchers use Claude
items.body: Anthropic studied 207,049 research sessions with Claude and Claude Code. Use was heaviest in computer science, mathematics and statistics, mostly for analysing data and writing. The company suggests research output in some fields could grow considerably as these tools spread.

items.title: Practise the way you'll perform
items.body: Memory works best when practice resembles the moment you'll need it, an idea researchers call transfer-appropriate processing. If you'll need to explain a design aloud, rehearse by explaining it aloud, not just by re-reading notes.
items.hook: Wonder: does your practice look like your real test?

items.title: Java: HashMap makes no promise about order
items.body: Iterating a HashMap can return keys in any order, and that order can change as the map grows. If you need insertion order, use LinkedHashMap; if you need sorted keys, use TreeMap. Tests that pass 'by luck' on HashMap order are a classic slow-burning bug.
items.q: Which Java map keeps keys in insertion order?
items.a: LinkedHashMap.

items.title: Pin or skewer?
items.body: Both are attacks along a line. In a pin, the piece in front is the less valuable one, and it can't move without exposing something bigger behind it. In a skewer, the valuable piece is in front; it has to step aside, and the piece behind it falls.
items.q: In a skewer, is the more valuable piece in front or behind?
items.a: In front: it must move, exposing the piece behind it.

items.title: The last seat on the ferry
items.body: She took the last seat on the ferry, next to a man holding a potted lemon tree. Halfway across, the wind turned and the boat rocked. Without a word, they each put a hand on the pot. On the far side he nodded, she nodded, and they walked off in different directions. She smelled lemon leaves on her fingers all afternoon.

items.title: A gas that hints Mars may not be fully asleep
items.body: Scientists report traces of hydrogen chloride in the Martian air, a gas that on Earth often comes from volcanoes. It could hint at recent volcanic activity on Mars, though the researchers are careful to call it a maybe.
items.hook: Wonder: how do you take the pulse of a planet from orbit?

items.title: Grapes take their time
items.body: No great thing is created suddenly, any more than a bunch of grapes or a fig.

items.title: Sea otters have pockets
items.body: Sea otters have a loose pouch of skin under each foreleg. They use it to carry food up from the sea floor, and often a favourite rock they use to crack open shells.
items.hook: Wonder: what would you keep in your own built-in pocket?

items.title: The first .com
items.body: The first .com domain name ever registered was symbolics.com, on 15 March 1985, by Symbolics, a company that made computers for running the Lisp language. For a while, registering a domain was a quiet, almost clerical act.
items.q: What was the first .com domain registered?
items.a: symbolics.com, in March 1985.

items.title: Ai2 teaches robot arms with toy blocks
items.body: The Allen Institute for AI released ToyBlocks, an open robot-arm simulator with 85,336 automatically generated demonstrations, about 1,600 hours of practice. Policies trained only in simulation did well on simple skills, though moving blocks to new places still trips them up. The training code and weights are open.
items.q: Roughly how many hours of demonstrations come with Ai2's ToyBlocks?
items.a: About 1,600 hours (85,336 demonstrations).

items.title: Ellora's Kailasa: a temple carved from the top down
items.body: Cave 16 at Ellora, the Kailasa temple, was cut out of a single basalt hillside in the 8th century, traditionally credited to the Rashtrakuta king Krishna I. The builders worked downward from the top of the rock, removing stone to reveal courtyards, shrines and towers, so there was no room for a misplaced cut.
items.hook: Wonder: how do you plan a building you can only subtract from?

items.title: Snowflake IDs: unique and roughly in time order
items.body: Twitter's Snowflake scheme builds a 64-bit ID from three parts: a millisecond timestamp (41 bits), a machine number (10 bits) and a per-millisecond counter (12 bits). Each machine can mint IDs without asking anyone, and sorting the IDs sorts them roughly by creation time.
items.q: What are the three parts of a Snowflake ID?
items.a: A timestamp, a machine ID and a sequence counter.

items.title: The peak-end rule
items.body: Research led by Daniel Kahneman found that people tend to remember an experience mostly by its most intense moment and by how it ended, rather than by its total length. A practical use: end a study or work session on something you can do well, so the memory of the session, and your wish to return, stays warm.
items.q: According to the peak-end rule, which two moments shape how we remember an experience?
items.a: The most intense moment (the peak) and the ending.

items.title: Set the 'good enough' line first
items.body: Before you start, write one sentence describing what 'done enough' looks like for this task. When you reach it, stop and call it finished. Perfectionism often hides inside tasks with no clear edge; a written edge makes stopping feel allowed.
items.hook: Wonder: how much of a task is the last 10% of polish?

items.title: Sunday, before anyone wakes
items.body:
The milk packet waits by the door,
cold and patient.
A crow says one word
and decides that is enough.
I do the same.

items.title: G.N. Gopal leads in Bavaria
items.body: Indian GM G.N. Gopal is sole leader of the Bavarian Championship at Tegernsee with 5½ out of 6, after beating 15-year-old German IM Hussain Besou in round six. Twelve players sit half a point behind, so the final rounds should be lively.
items.q: What was G.N. Gopal's score after six rounds at Tegernsee?
items.a: 5½ out of 6.

items.title: A dead star with two rings of debris
items.body: Astronomers have found a white dwarf, the cooled core of a Sun-like star, circled by two separate rings of planetary debris with a gap between them. It offers a possible glimpse of what our own Solar System might look like billions of years from now, once the Sun has settled into a white dwarf.
items.q: What kind of star is circled by the newly found double ring?
items.a: A white dwarf, the leftover core of a Sun-like star.

items.title: Anthropic sketches how agents could remember
items.body: In a research post, Anthropic split agent memory into three layers: notes the agent writes while it works, a stronger model that decides which of those notes are worth keeping, and a tidying-up pass during idle time that the team calls "dreaming". The idea is that memory improves when it is reviewed, not just stored.
items.hook: Wonder: what would you keep if you reviewed today's notes before bed?

items.title: Night auto
items.body:
The meter ticks in rupees and in stars.
The driver hums an old film tune, off-key,
and the city, for once, does not argue.
At my gate he says, 'Slowly, sir,'
as if the last three steps
were the hard part.

items.title: Quick retrieval: this edition
items.body: Try to answer from memory before peeking: How many chunks can working memory hold for most adults? What was hiding in Webb's images of 51 Eridani? Which company ran LEO I?
items.q: Three answers?
items.a: About four chunks; the gas giant 51 Eridani b; J. Lyons & Co., the tea-shop company.

items.title: Ask the agent to point at the line
items.body: When an agent tells you what a document or codebase says, ask it to quote the exact line and say where it came from. It costs a few words and turns 'trust me' into 'see for yourself'. If it can't find the line, that's useful to know too.

items.title: The biggest desert is cold
items.body: A desert is defined by how little precipitation it gets, not by heat. By that measure Antarctica, at about 14 million square kilometres, is the largest desert on Earth, larger than the Sahara.
items.hook: Wonder: what other words do we picture wrongly because of one famous example?

items.title: Luft: give your king air
items.body: After castling, a king boxed in by its own pawns can be mated by a single rook or queen on the back rank. Players often push a pawn one square, like h3 or g3, to give the king a 'luft' (German for air): a breathing square to step into. Do it at a calm moment, not when you're under attack.
items.q: What does 'luft' mean, and why make it?
items.a: German for 'air'; a pawn move that gives the king an escape square against back-rank mates.

items.title: Two-phase commit, gently
items.body: When several databases must all commit or all cancel, two-phase commit uses a coordinator. Phase one: it asks everyone 'can you commit?' and each participant prepares and votes. Phase two: if all vote yes, it says 'commit'; otherwise 'abort'. The catch: if the coordinator goes quiet after the votes, prepared participants have to wait, which is why many systems prefer sagas for long workflows.
items.hook: Wonder: what's the everyday version of 'everyone say yes before we book the tickets'?

items.title: Saying and doing
items.body: Saying is easy for anyone. Doing what you said, that is the rare thing.

items.title: A tea shop built a business computer
items.body: In 1951 J. Lyons & Co., a British chain of tea shops and bakeries, ran what is often called the world's first routine business job on its own computer, LEO I. The early tasks included valuing the bakeries' output. A company that sold cakes and tea helped invent business computing.
items.q: What kind of company built LEO I?
items.a: J. Lyons & Co., a British tea-shop and bakery company.

items.title: Let the place push back
items.body: A setting is more than a backdrop. Let it make things a little harder: a power cut during the important call, rain that won't let the letter dry, a lift that only goes to the third floor. Small resistance from the world gives your character something to do, and reveals who they are when they do it.

items.title: That bright 'star' at dawn is Venus
items.body: If you're up before sunrise, look low in the east: the brilliant point of light is Venus, now back in the morning sky. It keeps brightening through November toward its peak. Its glow comes from thick, reflective clouds that bounce back most of the sunlight that hits them.
items.q: Why does Venus shine so brightly?
items.a: Its thick clouds reflect most of the sunlight that reaches it.

items.title: Cursor's agent can now ship a small web app
items.body: Cursor's cloud agent can now build a web app from plain-language instructions, set up a database and sign-in, and deploy it to a shareable link. Security checks run before anything goes live, and you have to approve the deployment yourself. It's available on paid plans with cloud agents turned on.
items.hook: Wonder: what tiny app have you wanted for years but never had an afternoon for?

items.title: Tolkappiyam, the old grammar of Tamil
items.body: The Tolkappiyam is the oldest surviving work of Tamil grammar. Beyond letters and words, its third book covers poetics: landscapes, themes and how poems express feeling. Scholars still debate its exact date, but it shaped how Tamil literature was read for centuries.
items.q: Besides letters and words, what does the Tolkappiyam's third book cover?
items.a: Poetics: subject matter, landscapes and how poems carry meaning.

items.title: Try a sound backdrop
items.body: Some people with ADHD focus better with steady background sound: brown noise, rain, or the hum of a café. The research is mixed and it doesn't suit everyone, so treat it as an experiment: try it for one work block, notice how it feels, and keep it only if it helps.

items.title: Let a view of green restore you
items.body: Attention Restoration Theory, from Rachel and Stephen Kaplan, suggests that natural scenes hold our attention gently, so the effortful, focused kind of attention gets to rest. Several studies find small improvements on attention tasks after time in nature. Even a few minutes by a window with trees is a reasonable, pleasant experiment.

items.title: Sea stars run without a brain
items.body: Starfish have no brain. A ring of nerves around the mouth links a nerve cord in each arm, and the arms coordinate well enough to choose a direction and crawl. They also see with a simple eye spot at the tip of each arm.
items.hook: Wonder: who's in charge when every arm can vote?

items.title: Java: List.of vs Collections.unmodifiableList
items.body: Collections.unmodifiableList(list) gives you a read-only view: you can't change it, but if someone changes the original list, the view changes too. List.of(...) (Java 9+) builds a truly immutable list that has no backing list, and it refuses null elements. Reach for List.of (or List.copyOf) when you want 'this will never change'.
items.q: Does an unmodifiableList view change if the underlying list changes?
items.a: Yes. It's only a read-only view; List.of/List.copyOf make a real immutable copy.

items.title: World Junior Rapid crowns its champions
items.body: The FIDE World Junior Rapid Championship finished in Al Ain, UAE. Uzbekistan's GM Khumoyun Begmuratov won the open section unbeaten on 7.5/9, and Eline Roebers of the Netherlands won the girls' title with 7/9. The event drew 185 players from 40 countries.
items.q: Who won the girls' title in Al Ain?
items.a: Eline Roebers of the Netherlands, with 7/9.

items.title: The sign painter's last letter
items.body: Every shop on the street had his letters: the bakery's curly B, the chemist's steady capitals. When he retired, the shopkeepers asked him for one more sign, for his own door. He thought for a week and painted only one word, in his plainest hand: 'Open.' He never said which way he meant it. People still stop to chat there.

items.title: Send your name to Titan
items.body: NASA is inviting the public to send their names to Saturn's moon Titan aboard Dragonfly, the rotorcraft that will fly between spots on Titan's surface. If the schedule holds, it is planned to begin exploring Titan in 2034. Titan is the only moon with a thick atmosphere, which is what makes flying there possible.
items.hook: Wonder: what does it feel like to know your name is resting on a moon with methane rain?

items.title: Thinking Machines releases Inkling 2 Small
items.body: Thinking Machines Lab released Inkling 2 Small, a model aimed at coding, visual tasks and longer autonomous work. It has 594 billion parameters in total but uses only about 17 billion for each request, a mixture-of-experts design. Developers can try it through the Tinker platform now, with downloadable weights planned after more safety testing.
items.q: Roughly how many of Inkling 2 Small's parameters are active per request?
items.a: About 17 billion (of 594 billion total).

items.title: The little candle
items.body:
How far that little candle throws his beams!
So shines a good deed in a naughty world.
items.who: William Shakespeare, The Merchant of Venice

items.title: UTF-8 was sketched on a diner placemat
items.body: In September 1992, Ken Thompson and Rob Pike worked out the design of UTF-8 over dinner at a New Jersey diner, by Pike's account on a placemat. Its clever trick: plain ASCII text is already valid UTF-8, so old files kept working while the world's scripts, including Tamil, got room to fit.
items.q: Why could old ASCII files survive the move to UTF-8?
items.a: Every ASCII byte is already valid UTF-8 with the same meaning.

items.title: About four things at once
items.body: Working memory, the mental desk where you juggle ideas, holds far less than the old 'seven plus or minus two' suggests. Psychologist Nelson Cowan's work points to about four chunks for most adults. That's why writing a step down, or grouping items into bigger chunks, makes hard thinking feel lighter.
items.hook: Wonder: which four things are on your mental desk right now?

items.title: Everest's summit was once seabed
items.body: The rock at the very top of Mount Everest is marine limestone, and it contains fossils of sea creatures such as trilobites and crinoids. It formed on an ancient ocean floor and was lifted more than eight kilometres as India pressed into Asia.
items.q: What kind of rock is at Everest's summit?
items.a: Marine limestone, with fossils of ancient sea life.

items.title: Konark, a temple shaped like a chariot
items.body: The Sun Temple at Konark in Odisha, built in the 13th century under the Eastern Ganga king Narasimhadeva I, was designed as the Sun god's chariot: 24 carved stone wheels along its base, drawn by seven stone horses. It is a UNESCO World Heritage Site, and its wheel appears on India's ₹10 note.
items.hook: Wonder: how do you carve motion into something meant to stand still for centuries?

items.title: Power of two choices
items.body: A simple load-balancing trick: instead of sending a request to one random server, pick two at random and send it to the less busy one. That tiny comparison dramatically reduces how overloaded the worst server gets, compared with pure random choice, and it needs no global view of the whole cluster.
items.q: In 'power of two choices', how many servers do you sample per request?
items.a: Two, chosen at random; send to the less loaded one.

items.title: The one-box reset
items.body: When a desk is too cluttered to start, don't tidy it. Sweep everything into one box, set it aside, and start working on the clear surface. Sort the box later, one item at a time, when you have spare energy. A clear surface now beats a perfect system someday.
items.hook: Wonder: how much of 'I can't start' is really 'I can't see where to start'?

items.title: Yakubboev takes Freestyle Friday
items.body: GM Nodirbek Yakubboev won the November 6 Freestyle Friday with 9.5 points, half a point ahead of GM Ian Nepomniachtchi. It's his second Freestyle Friday title this year. In Freestyle (Chess960) the back-rank pieces are shuffled, so memorised openings help much less.
items.q: Who finished half a point behind Yakubboev?
items.a: Ian Nepomniachtchi, on 9 points.

items.title: Saturday, late
items.body:
The week folds itself
like a newspaper nobody finished.
On the sill, the tulsi
keeps its own small hours.
I leave one light on —
not for anyone,
just so the night
has somewhere to rest its eyes.

items.title: Webb finds a planet that was hiding in plain sight
items.body: 51 Eridani b, a young gas giant about 11 times Jupiter's mass and roughly 97 light-years away, was spotted from the ground in 2015 but kept disappearing in Webb's images. A Northwestern team built a 'digital twin' of the telescope to subtract the star's glare precisely, and the planet stepped out of the dark. The method, called FLIP, was published in Nature this week.
items.q: What did the team build to remove the starlight?
items.a: A physics-based digital twin of the telescope (the FLIP method).

items.title: Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash makes longer video clips
items.body: Google released Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash, its fast video model. Clips can now run up to 15 seconds instead of 10, you can refine a clip with follow-up prompts, and the price dropped about 30% to $0.07 per second of 720p video.
items.hook: Wonder: what would you film if a 15-second clip cost less than a cup of tea?

items.title: Window seat
items.body:
The train hums its one long note.
Fields go by in no hurry,
a boy waves from a bicycle,
a heron forgets us mid-step.
I had a list in my pocket.
Somewhere after the third bridge
it became a bookmark,
then nothing at all.

items.title: Old windows aren't melting
items.body: You may have heard that old church windows are thicker at the bottom because glass slowly flows. It doesn't, not on any human timescale. Old panes were made by spinning molten glass into uneven discs, and glaziers often set the heavier edge downward. At room temperature, a visible sag would take far longer than the age of the universe.
items.hook: Wonder: if glass isn't flowing, what makes it different from a crystal like quartz?

items.title: Let the agent read before it writes
items.body: Before asking a coding agent to change anything, ask it to read the relevant files and tell you in a few lines how they fit together. If its summary is wrong, you've caught the misunderstanding before it became a diff. Cheap reading saves expensive undoing.
Those who plan will gain what they planned, just as they planned it, if they stay firm in the doing.

items.title: Lamport clocks: ordering without a wall clock
items.body: Servers' clocks drift, so timestamps can lie. A Lamport clock is just a counter: bump it on every event, send it with every message, and when you receive one, set yours to max(yours, theirs) + 1. Now if A caused B, A's number is always smaller, no synchronised watches needed.
items.q: On receiving a message, how does a node update its Lamport clock?
items.a: Set it to max(own counter, message's counter) + 1.

items.title: Take an awe walk
items.body: In a 2020 study, older adults who took weekly 15-minute walks while deliberately noticing things that amazed them, like the size of trees or the colour of the sky, reported more positive feelings than those who simply walked. Their selfies also showed them taking up less of the frame, as if the world had grown bigger.

items.title: Zwischenzug: the in-between move
items.body: When your opponent expects an obvious recapture, look first for a stronger move in between, often a check or a threat that must be answered. Only then do you recapture, with a better position. The German word means 'intermediate move'. Before any 'automatic' move, ask: is there something more forcing first?
items.q: What is a zwischenzug?
items.a: An in-between move, often a check or threat, played instead of the expected reply before returning to it.

items.title: Why email uses @
items.body: In 1971 Ray Tomlinson sent the first networked email between two computers on ARPANET sitting side by side. He needed a symbol to separate a person's name from their machine and picked @, because it was on the keyboard and almost never appeared in names. User 'at' host.
items.hook: Wonder: what do other languages call the @ sign? (Italian: chiocciola, the snail.)

items.title: Mars overtakes Jupiter before dawn
items.body: Look east in the hours before sunrise this month: Mars and Jupiter climb high near the Sickle of Leo. On 16 November Mars slides past Jupiter, and on 26 November it passes the star Regulus. Later in the month Mercury joins the dawn too, best seen around 16–26 November.
items.q: On what date does Mars pass Jupiter in the November dawn sky?
items.a: 16 November.

items.title: Three things, not thirty
items.body: A long to-do list can feel like a wall of noise. Each morning, copy just three items onto a small card. Finish those and anything extra is a bonus. The full list still exists; it just doesn't get to shout at you all day.

items.title: The neighbourhood map
items.body: Meena drew a map of her street for a school project and, being thorough, marked everything: the dog that waits by gate 14, the bench where the old men argue about cricket, the mango tree that drops fruit on Tuesdays (it doesn't, but it felt like it). Her teacher gave it a B. The street gave it a frame. It hangs in the tea stall now, and strangers study it as if it were a country.

items.title: Rani ki Vav, a stepwell like an upside-down temple
items.body: In Patan, Gujarat, Rani ki Vav is an 11th-century stepwell associated with Queen Udayamati. Its terraces step down several storeys to the water, lined with hundreds of carved sculptures. It became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2014 and appears on the back of India's lavender ₹100 note.
items.q: Which Indian banknote shows Rani ki Vav?
items.a: The ₹100 note (the lavender series).

items.title: Ask a decade of satellite photos a question
items.body: Planet introduced an AI app that lets people search around ten years of its satellite imagery in plain language, rather than by coordinates and dates alone. Think 'new solar farms near this river' instead of hunting through tiles by hand.
items.hook: Wonder: what slow change near your own town would you want to watch from above?

items.title: Learn an idea through three examples
items.body: An abstract idea sticks better when you see it in several different concrete cases, then notice what they share. One example teaches the example; three varied ones teach the idea. When you learn something new today, hunt for two more places it shows up.

items.title: Crows remember faces
items.body: Researchers at the University of Washington wore a particular mask while briefly catching and banding crows. For years afterwards, crows on campus scolded anyone wearing that mask, and even crows that never saw the original catching joined in. They seem to learn faces, and pass the lesson along.
items.q: What did the University of Washington mask study show about crows?
items.a: They recognise individual human faces for years and can learn from other crows which faces to watch.

items.title: Nakamura opens with eight straight wins
items.body: In Thursday's three 3+0 blitz events on Chess.com, Hikaru Nakamura won the first tournament with 10/11 after winning his first eight games. Parham Maghsoodloo took the second, and Sina Movahed won the third for his first title since March.

items.title: Java 21: switch that understands shapes
items.body: With pattern matching for switch (final in Java 21), you can switch on a type and bind it in one step: case Circle c -> Math.PI * c.r() * c.r(); case Square s -> s.side() * s.side();. Pair it with a sealed interface and the compiler can tell you when you've forgotten a case.
items.hook: Wonder: what bug disappears when the compiler checks that every case is covered?

items.title: Let dialogue sidestep
items.body: Real people rarely answer the question they were asked. 'Did you get the job?' 'Want some tea?' The dodge tells the reader more than a straight answer could. Try letting one character in your next scene answer a different question than the one asked.

items.title: White dwarfs that may stretch a famous limit
items.body: A white dwarf normally can't be heavier than about 1.4 Suns, the Chandrasekhar limit, or it can no longer hold itself up. New simulations suggest that very strong magnetic fields might help some white dwarfs carry a little more mass than that. It's a model result for now, waiting for observations to test it.
items.q: Roughly what is the Chandrasekhar limit for a white dwarf?
items.a: About 1.4 times the Sun's mass.

items.body: Everywhere means nowhere.

items.title: Spacewar! (1962)
items.body: At MIT in 1962, Steve Russell and friends wrote Spacewar! on a PDP-1: two little ships circling a star whose gravity pulled on them. It's one of the earliest video games, and because its code was shared freely, copies spread to computer labs across the country.
items.q: On what computer was Spacewar! first written?
items.a: The DEC PDP-1, at MIT.

items.title: Perplexity introduces always-on 'Teammates'
items.body: Perplexity launched Teammates, agents meant to keep working in the background on ongoing work tasks instead of answering one question and stopping. They start with Max subscribers on the web. The interesting shift: agents designed as colleagues with standing jobs, not one-off chats.

items.title: Thanjavur's palace library
items.body: The Saraswati Mahal Library in Thanjavur grew from a royal collection of the Nayak kings and was greatly expanded by the Maratha ruler Serfoji II in the early 1800s. It holds thousands of palm-leaf and paper manuscripts in Tamil, Sanskrit, Marathi and other languages, and is counted among the oldest libraries in Asia.
items.q: Which ruler greatly expanded Thanjavur's Saraswati Mahal Library in the early 1800s?
items.a: Serfoji II.

items.title: Start in the middle
items.body: If the beginning of a task is the wall, skip it. Write the second paragraph first, fix the easy bug before the hard one, clean the one shelf you can see. Momentum built anywhere tends to carry you back to the start.

items.title: You can't see the Great Wall from orbit
items.body: A popular myth says the Great Wall of China is visible to the naked eye from space. It's very long but only a few metres wide and close in colour to the land around it. Astronauts in low Earth orbit, including China's first, Yang Liwei, have said they couldn't pick it out unaided.
items.hook: Wonder: what human-made things can astronauts see? (Hint: city lights at night.)

items.title: Quorums: R + W > N
items.body: Store each item on N replicas. Wait for W of them to confirm a write, and ask R of them on a read. If R + W > N, every read group overlaps every write group in at least one replica, so a read always touches someone who saw the latest write. N=3, W=2, R=2 is the classic, gentle choice.
items.q: With N=3 replicas, why do W=2 and R=2 give you fresh reads?
items.a: Because 2 + 2 > 3, any read set overlaps any write set in at least one replica that has the latest value.

items.title: The curse of knowledge
items.body: In a 1990 Stanford study, people tapped out the rhythm of well-known songs and guessed listeners would name about half. Listeners got roughly 1 in 40. The tappers could hear the melody in their heads; the listeners heard only knocks. Once you know something, it's hard to remember what not knowing felt like, so explain one step slower than feels necessary.
items.q: What is the 'curse of knowledge'?
items.a: Once you know something, it becomes hard to imagine not knowing it, so you overestimate how clear your explanation is.

items.title: Chess returns to the Esports World Cup in 2027
items.body: Chess.com confirmed chess will be back at the Esports World Cup next summer in Riyadh, where Magnus Carlsen will try for a third title after winning in 2025 and 2026. Qualification runs through the revamped Champions Chess Tour, with places also handed out via a points leaderboard built from Titled Tuesday, the Speed Chess Championship and the Chess.com Open.

items.title: Ironing
items.body:
Sunday, and the iron sighs
across a cotton shirt.
Each crease I press away
is a small week ending:
the bus, the rain, the long meeting,
all folded flat and warm,
hung on the door
like a promise to try again.

items.title: Airbnb plans a travel agent for 2027
items.body: Airbnb's Brian Chesky says the company plans to launch an AI travel agent in the first half of 2027. The idea is a helper that can sort out bookings and smooth over small problems during a stay, rather than just a search box with a chat window.
items.q: When does Airbnb plan to launch its AI travel agent?
items.a: In the first half of 2027.

items.title: A spacewalk with Earth as the backdrop
items.body: On 29 October, Canadian astronaut Joshua Kutryk paused mid-spacewalk for a photo with the blue Earth behind him, about 430 km above the South Atlantic. It was Canada's first spacewalk since 2019; he and NASA's Anil Menon were fitting one of the station's new roll-out solar arrays. Once all eight new arrays are in, NASA expects the station to have roughly 30% more power.
items.hook: Wonder: how do you roll out a solar panel like a yoga mat in zero gravity?

items.title: A parliament of owls
items.body: A group of owls is often called a parliament—a name that comes from old English writing that pictured owls as wise. In real life most owls live alone or in pairs, so you rarely see a full parliament.
The earth holds up even those who dig into it. Bear with those who scorn you in the same way.

items.title: Quick retrieval: this edition
items.body: Close your eyes and try: Who designed the first emoji set? What does a wood frog fill its cells with? Which constellation owns Alpheratz? Answers are on the cards above—check after you guess.

items.title: Bookmark
items.body:
I left the story on page ninety
with a bus ticket as a hand to hold.
The people inside kept still all week,
mid-sentence, mid-step,
polite as guests,
waiting for me
to come back and let them breathe.

items.title: Java's var is still static typing
items.body: Since Java 10, var lets the compiler infer a local variable's type: var names = new ArrayList<String>(); The type is fixed at compile time, exactly as if you'd written it out. Use it where the right side already says the type; spell it out where it doesn't.
items.q: Does `var` in Java make a variable dynamically typed?
items.a: No. The type is inferred once at compile time and stays fixed.

items.title: An epic named after an anklet
items.body: Silappatikaram, attributed to Ilango Adigal, is one of the great epics of Tamil literature. Its story turns on a single anklet, and it moves through three kingdoms—Chola, Pandya and Chera—giving a vivid picture of early Tamil city life, music and trade.
items.hook: Wonder: why might a poet tie a whole epic to one small object?

items.title: Give each task a start sound
items.body: Pick one song or playlist that only plays when you start a certain kind of work. After a few days, pressing play becomes the cue, and your brain starts sliding into the task before you've argued with it.

items.title: The first emoji were 12 by 12 pixels
items.body: In 1999 Shigetaka Kurita designed a set of 176 tiny pictures for NTT Docomo's i-mode phones in Japan. Each fit in a 12×12 grid. The set is now in the collection of the Museum of Modern Art in New York.
items.q: How many emoji were in Shigetaka Kurita's 1999 set?

items.title: The Moon hid Jupiter for a while
items.body: On 3 November the Moon slid in front of Jupiter as seen from parts of Earth, an occultation that skywatchers photographed as the bright planet vanished behind the lunar edge and reappeared. The two meet again in the sky near the end of the month.

items.title: Give the scene a clock
items.body: A deadline makes ordinary moments lean forward: the train leaves at 6:40, the milk is about to boil over, the shop shutter is coming down. You don't need danger—just a small clock the reader can hear ticking.

items.title: METR: Anthropic models improving about twice as fast
items.body: The evaluation nonprofit METR published an estimate that the pace at which Anthropic's models gain the ability to complete certain long tasks is roughly double what it was a year ago. It's a measurement of specific tasks, not a claim that everything got twice as good.

items.title: Days used to be shorter
items.body: Earth's spin is very slowly braking, mostly because of tides raised by the Moon. Hundreds of millions of years ago a day was only around 21–22 hours long, so a year had more than 400 sunrises.
items.hook: Wonder: how do fossil corals record the number of days in an ancient year?

items.title: Timelines: fan out on write or on read?
items.body: For a feed, you can push each new post into every follower's list when it's written (fast reads, heavy writes) or assemble the feed when someone opens it (light writes, slower reads). Many systems mix both: push for most people, pull for accounts with millions of followers.
items.q: What is the main cost of fan-out-on-write for a social feed?
items.a: Every post must be written into every follower's timeline, which is heavy for very popular accounts.

items.title: Feedback you can use today
items.body: Feedback helps learning most when it says what to do next, not just whether you were right. 'Wrong' teaches little; 'your second step dropped a sign' teaches a lot. When you check your own work, look for the step, not the score.

items.title: The outside passed pawn is a decoy
items.body: In king-and-pawn endings, a passed pawn far from the other pawns is a quiet weapon. You push it, the enemy king must chase it, and while it's away your king walks in and eats the pawns it left behind.
items.q: Why is an outside passed pawn strong in king-and-pawn endings?
items.a: It drags the enemy king away, letting your king attack the pawns on the other side.

items.title: The key-cutter's extra
items.body: Every time he cut a key, the old man at the market cut a second one and hung it on a nail behind him. 'Whose are those?' a boy asked. 'Everyone forgets once,' he said, and went back to the grinding wheel. Years later the boy came back, locked out in the rain. The key was still there, a little dusty, waiting.

items.title: The Great Square borrows a star
items.body: Pegasus, the winged horse, is high in the evening sky now, marked by four stars in a big square. One corner, Alpheratz, officially belongs to the neighbouring constellation Andromeda—the horse shares a star with the princess.
items.q: Which constellation does Alpheratz, a corner of the Great Square, belong to?
items.a: Andromeda.

items.title: Small diffs keep you in the loop
items.body: Ask a coding agent for one small change at a time rather than a sweeping rewrite. A 30-line diff you can actually read is worth more than 600 lines you skim and hope about. Review speed, not generation speed, is usually the real limit.
items.hook: Wonder: how big a change can you review carefully in five minutes?

items.body: Look within. Within is the fountain of good, and it will ever bubble up, if thou wilt ever dig.

items.title: VisiCalc, the first PC spreadsheet
items.body: In 1979 Dan Bricklin and Bob Frankston released VisiCalc for the Apple II. Change one number and every dependent cell updated—on a personal computer. Many businesses bought an Apple II just to run it.
items.q: Which computer did VisiCalc first run on?
items.a: The Apple II (1979).

items.title: Tamil written on cave beds
items.body: Some of the oldest Tamil writing sits on rock beds in caves near Madurai, such as at Mangulam. Carved in Tamil-Brahmi script around the 2nd century BCE, the lines record gifts of shelters to Jain monks.
items.q: What script was used for the earliest Tamil cave inscriptions?
items.a: Tamil-Brahmi.

items.title: Think out loud
items.body: When a task won't hold still in your head, narrate it: 'Okay, first I open the file, then I find the date column…'. Saying steps aloud moves them out of working memory and into the room, where they're easier to follow. Quietly mumbling counts.

items.title: The frog that freezes for winter
items.body: North American wood frogs can freeze almost solid in winter. Their hearts stop, much of their body water turns to ice, and sugar floods their cells to protect them. In spring they thaw and hop off.
items.q: What does a wood frog load its cells with to survive freezing?
items.a: Glucose (sugar), which acts like an antifreeze.

items.title: ConcurrentHashMap.computeIfAbsent, gently
items.body: map.computeIfAbsent(key, k -> build(k)) on a ConcurrentHashMap runs atomically per key: two threads asking for the same missing key won't both build it. Keep the function short, and never let it modify the same map—other threads may be waiting on that key.
items.q: Why keep the function passed to ConcurrentHashMap.computeIfAbsent short?
items.a: It runs while that key's entry is locked; other threads updating it wait, and it must not modify the map itself.

items.title: College chess heads to the playoffs
items.body: In the Collegiate Chess League, Saint Louis University and UT Dallas are locked in a close race for first place as the regular season winds down and the playoffs approach. University teams across the world play these matches online through the season.

items.title: Practise at the edge, not the middle
items.body: Deliberate practice means working just beyond what you can already do, with quick feedback, on one specific weakness. Playing through things you already handle well feels productive but teaches little. Pick the bar you keep fumbling, not the song you love.
items.hook: Wonder: which part of your skill do you quietly avoid practising?

items.title: Box builds a context layer for agents with Nvidia models
items.body: Box says it is using Nvidia's AI models to build a 'context layer' for enterprise agents: a way to hand an agent the right documents and background before it decides or acts. It's another sign that the hard part of agents is less the model and more what you feed it.
items.q: In agent design, what is a 'context layer' for?
items.a: Gathering the right information (documents, history, permissions) to give the agent before it acts.

items.title: The Sun is settling down
items.body: NOAA's sunspot count for October shows another sharp drop in Solar Cycle 25. After the busy peak of the last couple of years, our star is easing into the quieter half of its roughly 11-year rhythm.
items.hook: Wonder: what flips inside the Sun every 11 years or so? (Its magnetic poles.)

items.title: After the guests leave
items.body:
The last diya on the step
keeps talking to the dark
in a voice the size of a seed.

No one is listening now.
It does not seem to mind.
It was never burning for applause—
only for the next small circle of floor.

items.title: Evening, terrace
items.body:
Clothes on the line
lift their sleeves to the breeze.
A kite, very far, is someone's.
The first star says nothing,
which is enough.

items.title: Tardigrades survived open space
items.body: In 2007, tiny tardigrades rode outside a capsule in low Earth orbit, exposed to vacuum and cosmic radiation. Back on Earth, many of them revived and some even laid eggs. They survive by drying out and pausing their metabolism.
items.hook: Wonder: what does it feel like to pause, if you're a water bear?

items.title: Pause before the step you can't undo
items.body: A good agent design sorts actions into two piles: ones you can undo (drafting, reading, searching) and ones you can't (sending, paying, deleting). Let the agent run freely through the first pile and ask a person before anything in the second.
items.q: Which agent actions deserve a human check?
items.a: The irreversible ones: sending, paying, deleting.

items.title: Effort pays its wage
items.body: Even when fate will not allow a thing, honest effort still pays the wage of the work it took.

items.title: Chess began as chaturanga
items.body: The earliest known ancestor of chess, chaturanga, was played in India by around the 6th century CE. Its pieces stood for the four divisions of an army: infantry, cavalry, elephants and chariots. Those became pawns, knights, bishops and rooks.
items.hook: Wonder: which modern piece was once an elephant?

items.title: Retry with jitter
items.body: When a service hiccups, a thousand clients that all retry after exactly one second will knock it over again together. Exponential backoff waits longer after each failure, and jitter adds a little randomness so the retries spread out instead of arriving as one wave.
items.q: What does jitter add to retries?
items.a: Randomness in the wait, so clients don't retry in lockstep.

items.title: A two-day gathering for dark skies
items.body: DarkSky International holds 'Under One Sky', a free-to-join virtual conference on 6 and 7 November, about protecting night skies from light pollution. Shielded, warm-coloured outdoor lights that point down are one of the easiest fixes anyone can make.
items.hook: Wonder: when did you last see the Milky Way?

items.title: The first computer password
items.body: MIT's Compatible Time-Sharing System, started around 1961 under Fernando Corbató, let many people share one computer. Each user got private files, so each needed a password. It's widely credited as the first computer password system.
items.q: Why did CTSS need passwords?
items.a: Many users shared one machine and each had private files.

items.title: Call it a restart
items.body: Dropping a habit for a few days is normal for any brain, and common for ADHD brains. Instead of 'I failed again', try 'restart day'. Pick the smallest version of the habit, do it once today, and count that as the streak beginning again.

items.title: Rajaraja Chola measured the land
items.body: Around the start of the 11th century, the Chola king Rajaraja I ordered a detailed survey of farmland across his kingdom so that revenue could be assessed fairly. One of his titles, Ulagalanda, is often read as 'he who measured the world'.
items.hook: Wonder: how would you measure a kingdom with ropes and rods?

items.title: Cut your first paragraph
items.body: Many drafts warm up before they begin. Try deleting the opening paragraph and see if the piece starts better at the second. Often the first paragraph was for you, to find your way in; the reader can skip the stretching.

items.title: The Sahara used to be green
items.body: Between about 11,000 and 5,000 years ago, a wobble in Earth's orbit strengthened the African monsoon. The Sahara had lakes, grasslands, hippos and fishing villages. Rock art in the desert still shows cattle and swimmers.
items.q: What turned the Sahara green for thousands of years?
items.a: Small changes in Earth's orbit that strengthened the monsoon.

items.title: Meta picks up Conductor, a tool for running many coding agents
items.body: Meta acquired Conductor, a startup whose software lets a developer run several AI coding agents side by side, each on its own task. Terms weren't shared. It's another sign that the workflow is moving from one assistant to a small team of them.

items.title: When gut feelings can be trusted
items.body: Psychologists Daniel Kahneman and Gary Klein found common ground in 2009: intuition is reliable when the setting is regular enough to have patterns and you get quick, clear feedback on your guesses. A chess player's hunch qualifies; a guess about next year's stock prices doesn't.
items.hook: Wonder: where in your work do you get fast, honest feedback?

items.title: Doubts
items.body:
Our doubts are traitors,
And make us lose the good we oft might win
By fearing to attempt.

items.title: Rooks belong behind passed pawns
items.body: Tarrasch's rule: put your rook behind a passed pawn, yours or the opponent's. Behind your own pawn, the rook gains scope with every step the pawn takes. Behind the enemy pawn, it pins the pawn down without getting in the way.
items.q: Behind or in front: where should a rook go with a passed pawn?
items.a: Behind it, whichever side the pawn belongs to.

items.title: Dead-letter queues: a quiet shelf for stuck messages
items.body: If a message keeps failing, retrying it forever blocks everything behind it. A dead-letter queue moves it aside after a set number of attempts. The main flow keeps moving, and someone can inspect the shelf later, fix the cause and replay the message.
items.hook: Wonder: where is the dead-letter queue in your own week?

items.title: The left-luggage counter
items.body: The man at the station's left-luggage counter had kept the blue suitcase for eleven days. On the twelfth, a woman came with the ticket, out of breath. 'Sorry,' she said. 'I needed somewhere to put it while I decided.' He handed it over. 'And?' She smiled and lifted it easily. 'I'm keeping it.'

items.title: The loom that read cards
items.body: In 1804 Joseph Marie Jacquard's loom wove patterns from chains of punched cards: a hole let a hook through, no hole held it back. Charles Babbage borrowed the idea for his Analytical Engine, and Herman Hollerith's census machines later used punched cards too.
items.q: What did Jacquard's punched cards originally control?
items.a: The threads of a weaving loom.

items.title: Venus and Spica share the dawn
items.body: These mornings, look east before sunrise: brilliant Venus sits near Spica, the brightest star in Virgo. Spica is actually two hot blue stars orbiting each other in about four days, roughly 250 light-years away, while Venus is a few light-minutes from us.
items.hook: Wonder: the light from the two dots left them about 250 years apart. What was happening when Spica's light set out?

items.title: Name the alarm after the action
items.body: An alarm that just says '4:00' asks your brain to remember why it rang. Label it with the next physical step instead: 'Open laptop, reply to Priya.' When it goes off, the decision is already made and you only have to move.

items.title: The sundial as tall as a building
items.body: The Samrat Yantra at Jantar Mantar in Jaipur, built under Sawai Jai Singh II and completed in the 1730s, is a giant sundial whose triangular gnomon rises about 27 metres. Its shadow moves several centimetres a minute, so local solar time can be read to within a few seconds.
items.q: Who built the Jaipur Jantar Mantar?
items.a: Maharaja Sawai Jai Singh II.

items.title: Sierra buys Anon to help agents use websites
items.body: Customer-service AI company Sierra acquired Anon, whose browser-agent technology helps AI agents finish tasks on websites that don't offer an API. The idea: when there's no tidy back door, the agent can still walk through the front door like a person would.

items.title: Water can boil and freeze at the same time
items.body: At its triple point, about 0.01 °C and a pressure of around 0.6% of normal air pressure, water can exist as ice, liquid and vapour together in balance. In a vacuum chamber you can watch a dish of water bubble and frost over at once.
items.hook: Wonder: what would a cup of tea do on the summit of Mars?

items.title: Java text blocks: strings that keep their shape
items.body: Since Java 15, a text block starts with three double quotes and a newline. Inside, you can write JSON, SQL or HTML as it looks, without \n and escaped quotes everywhere. Java strips the common leading indentation, so the block can sit neatly indented in your code.
items.q: What opens a Java text block?
items.a: Three double quotes (""") followed by a line break.

items.title: Memory likes the room it was made in
items.body: In a 1975 study, divers learned word lists either on a beach or underwater. They recalled more when tested in the same place they had learned. The lesson for study isn't to always use one desk; it's the opposite: practise in a few different places so the knowledge isn't tied to one setting.
items.hook: Wonder: which of your skills only works at your own desk?

items.title: A 14-year-old earns a second GM norm
items.body: At the KazChess Masters, which Denis Lazavik won unbeaten, 14-year-old International Master Mark Smirnov picked up his second grandmaster norm. Three norms plus a 2500 rating make a grandmaster, so he is now one good tournament away from the final norm.
items.q: How many GM norms does a player usually need for the title?
items.a: Three, plus a rating of at least 2500.

items.title: Steel tumbler
items.body:
The tumbler sweats on the window sill,
holding a small cold sea.
Outside, the neem keeps still,
as if it, too, were thirsty.
I drink slowly. The afternoon
makes room.

items.title: Could neutrinos warn us before the Blaze Star flares?
items.body: T Coronae Borealis, the 'Blaze Star', is a recurrent nova: a white dwarf gathering gas from a companion star until a surface explosion makes it briefly bright enough to see without a telescope. It last did this in 1946. Astronomers are still waiting for the next outburst, and new research suggests a burst of neutrinos might arrive as an early heads-up.
items.q: In what year did the Blaze Star last erupt?
items.a: 1946 (and before that, 1866).

items.title: Microsoft Clarity starts counting AI-agent visitors
items.body: Microsoft's free website analytics tool, Clarity, added a view for visits made by AI agents rather than people. Site owners can see where an agent's automated journey through their pages went smoothly and where it got stuck or needed a check.
items.hook: Wonder: if half your visitors were agents, what would you redesign first?

items.title: Quick retrieval: this edition
items.body: Try answering before peeking: Who is Asia's first grandmaster? What does a heartbeat system listen for? What does WOOP stand for?
items.q: Who became Asia's first grandmaster, in 1974?
items.a: Eugenio Torre of the Philippines.

items.title: November, 6 pm
items.body:
The streetlights take their turns,
one, then the next, then all.
A boy stops kicking his ball
to watch the evening learn.

items.title: Lightning is hotter than the Sun's surface
items.body: A lightning bolt heats the air around it to roughly 30,000 °C for a split second, about five times the temperature of the Sun's visible surface. That sudden heating makes the air expand explosively, and the sound of it is thunder.
items.hook: Wonder: what's the longest gap you've counted between a flash and its thunder?

items.title: Philidor's third-rank defence
items.body: In a rook ending where you defend against king, rook and pawn, keep your king in front of the pawn and your rook on your third rank (the sixth from the attacker's side). The enemy king can't advance without help. The moment the pawn steps forward, swing your rook to the back and check from behind; the attacker's king now has no shelter.
items.q: In the Philidor defence, when does the defending rook go to the far side to check?
items.a: As soon as the attacking pawn advances to the defender's third rank.

items.title: Pick a shard key by how you read
items.body: When data is split across machines, the shard key decides where each row lives. Choose it from your most common query: if most reads ask 'everything for this customer', shard by customer so one machine can answer. A key that spreads writes evenly but scatters every read across all shards is a quiet performance trap.
items.q: What should mainly guide the choice of a shard key?
items.a: Your most common access pattern, so typical queries hit a single shard.

items.body: Seek not that the things which happen should happen as you wish; but wish the things which happen to be as they are, and you will have a tranquil flow of life.

items.title: Earth's shadow is in the sky tonight
items.body: Just after sunset, look east, opposite the Sun. A soft blue-grey band sits on the horizon: that is Earth's own shadow cast on the atmosphere. Above it glows a pink strip called the Belt of Venus. The same pair appears in the west just before sunrise.
items.hook: Wonder: when did you last look away from a sunset?

items.title: Give the scene a sound
items.body: Most drafts lean on sight. Before you finish a scene, ask what can be heard: a gate latch, rain on a tin roof, a pressure cooker's whistle two houses away. One true sound places the reader in the room faster than three sentences of description.

items.title: Where 'hello, world' came from
items.body: The tradition of a first program that prints 'hello, world' traces to Brian Kernighan. It appeared in his 1972 tutorial for the B language at Bell Labs and became famous through The C Programming Language (1978), which he wrote with Dennis Ritchie.
items.q: Which book made 'hello, world' famous?
items.a: The C Programming Language (1978) by Kernighan and Ritchie.

items.title: Map your good hours
items.body: For a week, jot a one-word energy note (high, okay, low) every couple of hours. Patterns appear quickly. Then put your hardest thinking in your high slots and save email, errands and tidying for the low ones. It's working with your brain instead of against it.
items.hook: Wonder: when in the day does your mind feel clearest?

items.title: Saturn is less dense than water
items.body: Saturn's average density is about 0.69 grams per cubic centimetre, lower than water's 1. That's the source of the famous line that it would float in a big enough bathtub, though as a ball of gas it would hardly hold together in one.
items.q: Which planet in our solar system has an average density lower than water?
items.a: Saturn.

items.title: Small tools beat one giant tool
items.body: When giving an agent tools, many small, clearly named ones usually work better than one tool with twenty optional settings. A narrow tool is easier for the model to choose correctly and easier for you to test. If two tools are always called together, that's the moment to combine them, not before.

items.title: Geometry with ropes: the Sulba Sutras
items.body: The Sulba Sutras, ancient Indian manuals for laying out fire altars, gave rules using stretched cords. Baudhayana's text states that the diagonal of a rectangle produces as much area as its two sides do separately, the relationship now known as the Pythagorean theorem. It also gives a remarkably close approximation of the square root of 2.
items.hook: Wonder: what could you build with only a rope and some pegs?

items.title: Mental contrasting: picture the wish, then the snag
items.body: Psychologist Gabriele Oettingen's research suggests pure positive daydreaming can sap drive. A better habit: imagine the outcome you want, then name the main inner obstacle, then plan what you'll do when it shows up. Her acronym is WOOP: Wish, Outcome, Obstacle, Plan.
items.q: What does WOOP stand for?
items.a: Wish, Outcome, Obstacle, Plan.

items.title: CompletableFuture: say what happens next
items.body: In Java, a CompletableFuture lets you describe follow-up steps instead of waiting. thenApply transforms a result, thenCompose chains another async call, and thenCombine joins two independent results. Call join() only at the very edge of your program, so threads aren't parked waiting in the middle.
items.q: When do you use thenCompose instead of thenApply?
items.a: When the next step itself returns a CompletableFuture, so you get a flat future instead of a nested one.

items.title: A 15-year-old shares the lead at Tegernsee
items.body: After five rounds of the Bavarian Championship in Gmund am Tegernsee, six players share first place on 4½ points, among them three Indian grandmasters. One of the leaders is 15-year-old German IM Hussain Besou, who beat former world junior champion Peter Acs in round five.

items.title: The piano tuner's last house
items.body: Every Thursday the tuner saved the old teacher's upright for last. It never really needed him; she kept it beautifully. But she made cardamom tea, and he played one slow piece before leaving, and she said each time that it sounded better than before. He let her think it was his doing. It was the tea.

items.title: Peanuts aren't nuts
items.body: Peanuts are legumes, cousins of peas and beans. The plant flowers above ground, then pushes its developing pods down into the soil, where the 'nuts' ripen.
items.q: What plant family do peanuts belong to?
items.a: The legumes (pea and bean family).

items.title: A year inside a pretend Mars
items.body: Four volunteers, Ross Elder, Ellen Ellis, Matthew Montgomery and James Spicer, stepped out of NASA's 3D-printed Mars habitat at Johnson Space Center in Houston on 31 October after more than a year inside. Messages to the outside world had built-in delays of 26 to 44 minutes, just like real Earth–Mars calls. It was the second of three planned CHAPEA missions.
items.hook: Wonder: what would you most miss after a year in a quiet Martian home?

items.body: It is not the man who has too little, but the man who craves more, that is poor.

items.title: ASCII: 128 characters to agree on
items.body: Before 1963, different machines used different codes for letters, so text didn't travel well. ASCII, first published in 1963, fixed a shared table using 7 bits, giving 128 slots for letters, digits, punctuation and control signals like 'carriage return'. Its first 128 characters still sit unchanged at the start of Unicode today.
items.q: How many characters does 7-bit ASCII define?
items.a: 128 (2 to the 7th power).

items.title: Agents that remember between runs
items.body: MongoDB has released an integration with Google's Agent Development Kit that stores an agent's sessions and memory in a database. The point is durability: an agent can pick up where it left off instead of starting every run from a blank slate.
items.hook: Wonder: what should an assistant remember about yesterday, and what should it let go?

items.title: Worked examples first, then fade them
items.body: When you're new to a skill, studying a fully solved example teaches more than struggling alone, because your working memory isn't swamped. As you improve, the benefit flips: experts learn more from solving problems themselves (the 'expertise reversal' effect). A gentle path is to start with complete examples, then gradually hide more of each step.
items.q: What is the expertise reversal effect?
items.a: Supports that help beginners, like worked examples, help less (or even hinder) as learners gain expertise.

items.title: Madras began with a land grant in 1639
items.body: In August 1639 the East India Company's Francis Day obtained a strip of coastal land where Fort St George was then built; the town that grew around it became Madras, today's Chennai. The city now marks Madras Day every year on 22 August.
items.q: Which fort was the seed of the city of Chennai?
items.a: Fort St George, begun after the 1639 land grant.

items.title: Let your body move while your mind works
items.body: Fidgeting isn't always a distraction. A 2015 study of children with ADHD found more movement went along with better working-memory performance during the task. Try a standing desk, a stress ball, or pacing while you think through a problem, and notice what actually helps you focus.
items.hook: Wonder: which small movement helps you think best?

items.title: Heartbeats: how a cluster notices silence
items.body: A node can't announce its own crash, so systems listen for the absence of a signal instead. Each node sends a small 'I'm alive' message every second or so; if several in a row go missing, others suspect it is down. The tuning is a trade: short timeouts detect failure fast but mistake a slow network for a dead node, long ones are calm but slow to react.
items.q: Why do heartbeat systems usually wait for several missed beats, not one?
items.a: A single missed beat is often just a slow or dropped message; waiting for several cuts false alarms.

items.title: Pressing flowers
items.body:
Between two pages of an atlas
a marigold went flat and gold.
Years later, looking up a river,
I found the morning it was sold.
items.hook: Wonder: what's tucked inside the books on your shelf?

items.title: Eugenio Torre, Asia's first grandmaster, turns 75
items.body: Born on 4 November 1951 in Iloilo City in the Philippines, Torre became the first Asian player to earn the grandmaster title in 1974. He holds the record for Chess Olympiad appearances, with 23. He was inducted into the World Chess Hall of Fame in 2021 and has a small personal chess museum near his home in Marikina City.
items.q: How many Chess Olympiads has Eugenio Torre played, a record?

items.title: Netflix tries picking shows by mood
items.body: Netflix has started testing 'AI Discover' on supported TVs in the US. Instead of typing a title, you choose a mood or situation, then narrow the suggestions with a few follow-up choices. Netflix calls it an experiment and will decide later what to expand.
items.hook: Wonder: would you rather describe a feeling or a genre when choosing what to watch?

items.title: Earth has a tiny new mini-moon: 2026 QQ8
items.body: A rock only about a metre across has been quietly circling Earth since around April. It was first spotted on 20 August by Krisztián Sárneczky, and follow-up telescope looks confirmed it is natural, most likely a small asteroid rather than old rocket hardware. It should stay with us through December, then drift off on its own path in 2027.
items.hook: Wonder: how many small 'moons' come and go without anyone noticing?
items.q: About how big is the mini-moon 2026 QQ8?
items.a: Roughly 1 metre (about 3 feet) across.

items.title: Ask the agent for its plan first
items.body: For any agent task that changes things, have it write out its plan before it acts: the steps, the files or systems it will touch, and how it will know it's done. Reading a plan takes a minute; untangling a confident wrong turn takes an afternoon.
items.hook: Wonder: which of your own tasks would go better if you wrote the plan first, too?

items.title: A knight on the rim
items.body: The old saying 'a knight on the rim is dim' has geometry behind it. In the centre a knight can reach eight squares; on an edge, at most four; in a corner, only two. It isn't a law, just a gentle nudge to ask, before you move a knight sideways, where it can go next.
items.q: How many squares can a knight reach from a corner?
items.a: Two.

items.title: Sagas: undo in small steps
items.body: When one business action spans several services, a single database transaction can't cover it all. A saga splits it into local steps, each with a matching 'compensating' step: book the room, then charge the card; if charging fails, cancel the room. You trade instant all-or-nothing for a clear, reliable path back.
items.q: In a saga, what replaces a rollback?
items.a: Compensating actions that undo each completed step.

items.title: Library, closing time
items.body:
The lights go off
one aisle at a time,
like someone saying
goodnight to each shelf.

The last reader
marks her page with a bus ticket
and leaves the story
waiting, mid-sentence, for her.

items.title: Bamboo you could almost watch grow
items.body: Some bamboo species can grow close to 90 centimetres in a single day, among the fastest-growing plants on Earth. Bamboo is a grass, so it's a very ambitious cousin of your lawn.
items.hook: Wonder: if you sat beside it all day, could you see it move?

items.title: The internet's flag day
items.body: On 1 January 1983, the ARPANET switched over to the TCP/IP protocols in one planned changeover, often called 'flag day'. Machines that hadn't made the switch could no longer talk on the network. The protocols adopted that day still carry most internet traffic.
items.q: On what date did the ARPANET switch to TCP/IP?
items.a: 1 January 1983.

items.body: Some things are in our control and others not.

items.title: ESCAPADE twins swing past Earth on the way to Mars
items.body: NASA's two ESCAPADE spacecraft, built to study how Mars loses its upper atmosphere, are each due to make a powered flyby of Earth, firing their engines during the close pass to pick up speed toward Mars. NASA says this kind of manoeuvre is a first for its spacecraft.
items.q: What will the ESCAPADE twins study at Mars?
items.a: How Mars' upper atmosphere is stripped away into space.

items.title: Put the task where you'll trip over it
items.body: Out of sight really can mean out of mind. Leave the parcel to post by the front door, the library book on your shoes, the form on top of your laptop. Let your surroundings do the remembering, so your head doesn't have to.

items.title: Panini's grammar in about 4,000 rules
items.body: The Sanskrit grammarian Panini, usually dated to around the 4th century BCE (scholars still debate the exact time), described the whole language in the Ashtadhyayi, nearly 4,000 compact rules. Its rules call one another and build words step by step, which is why linguists and computer scientists still admire it as an early formal system.
items.hook: Wonder: was the Ashtadhyayi, in a way, one of the world's first programs?

items.title: Meta ships ML features 3.6× faster
items.body: Meta's engineering team describes F3 Lightning, a system in its ads infrastructure where each machine-learning feature compiles, validates, deploys and rolls back on its own. Meta reports comparable features now reach production about 3.6 times faster, with no increase in compute cost.

items.title: Leases: a lock that expires
items.body: In a distributed system, a plain lock is dangerous: if its holder crashes, nobody can get it back. A lease is a lock with an expiry time. The holder must keep renewing it; if it goes quiet, the lease lapses and someone else can take over. Pair it with an increasing 'fencing token' so a slow old holder can't overwrite the new one's work.
items.q: Why use a lease instead of a plain lock?
items.a: It expires if the holder stops renewing it, so a crashed holder can't block everyone forever.

items.title: The umbrella that came back
items.body: Every monsoon the corner tea stall kept a bucket of forgotten umbrellas. Anyone could borrow one. Most never came back, and the old man never minded. One July a girl returned a faded green umbrella he'd lent her six years earlier. 'I'm a teacher now,' she said. 'My school has a bucket too.' He put the green one back in his own, right at the front.

items.title: Familiar isn't the same as learned
items.body: Rereading notes makes them feel familiar, and familiarity feels like knowing. Psychologists call this a fluency illusion. A gentler test: close the page and try to explain it in your own words. Whatever you can't recall is exactly what to look at again, and that's useful, not a failure.
items.q: What is the 'fluency illusion'?
items.a: Mistaking the easy familiarity of rereading for actually having learned something.

items.title: Polar bears have black skin
items.body: Under that white coat, a polar bear's skin is black. The fur hairs themselves aren't white either; they're translucent, and they look white because they scatter light, much the way snow does.
items.hook: Wonder: what other 'colours' in nature are really just scattered light?

items.title: The wrong-coloured bishop
items.body: King, bishop and a rook's pawn (an a- or h-pawn) against a lone king can be a draw. If the bishop can't control the pawn's promotion square, and the defending king reaches that corner, it simply cannot be driven out. An extra bishop and pawn, and still no win: endgames love a quiet surprise.
items.q: When is king + bishop + rook's pawn vs king a draw?
items.a: When the bishop doesn't control the promotion square and the defending king reaches that corner.

items.title: Where the word 'bit' came from
items.body: The word 'bit', short for 'binary digit', was coined by statistician John Tukey. Claude Shannon used it in his landmark 1948 paper on information theory and credited Tukey for the word, and it has been the smallest unit of information ever since.
items.q: Who coined the word 'bit'?
items.a: John Tukey; Claude Shannon popularised it in 1948.

items.title: Vary the length of your sentences
items.body: A paragraph of same-length sentences reads like a metronome. Mix them. Let one sentence run long, gathering detail, letting the reader settle into its current. Then stop. The short one lands because the long one came first.

items.title: Betelgeuse's hidden companion leaves a wake
items.body: Astronomers say they have new evidence that a small, hidden companion star, named Siwarha, is moving through the outer atmosphere of the red supergiant Betelgeuse and stirring it up. That may explain some of the star's long-puzzling ripples and changes.
items.q: What is the name given to Betelgeuse's hidden companion star?
items.a: Siwarha.

items.body: Such as are thy habitual thoughts, such also will be the character of thy mind; for the soul is dyed by the thoughts.

items.title: Speech recognition that doesn't transcribe itself
items.body: Soniox has launched STT v6, a speech-to-text model covering more than 60 languages. For voice agents, it can take the agent's own spoken text as context and filter that audio out of the incoming stream, so the assistant doesn't end up transcribing its own voice. Real-time and batch versions are available.
items.hook: Wonder: how do you teach a machine to tell its own voice from yours?

items.title: Choose a stopping point before you start
items.body: Hyperfocus is easy to enter and hard to leave. Before you begin, decide where you'll stop: 'after this function', 'when the timer rings', 'at the end of this chapter'. Write it on a sticky note. A pre-chosen exit makes stopping feel like finishing, not like being interrupted.

items.title: Arikamedu, a Roman trading port near Puducherry
items.body: Around two thousand years ago, Arikamedu on the coast near present-day Puducherry was a busy trading town. Excavations, including Mortimer Wheeler's in 1945, found pieces of Roman wine jars and fine Mediterranean pottery alongside local beads, signs of a long sea trade between Tamil coasts and the Roman world.
items.hook: Wonder: what did a Roman sailor think of his first plate of Tamil food?

items.title: Java streams are lazy on purpose
items.body: In a Java Stream, filter and map don't do anything when you call them; they only describe the work. Nothing runs until a terminal operation such as collect, count or findFirst. That's why stream.filter(...).findFirst() can stop after the first match instead of scanning the whole list.
items.q: When does a Java stream's filter actually run?
items.a: Only when a terminal operation (collect, count, findFirst…) is called.

items.title: A cloud can weigh as much as a hundred elephants
items.body: The US Geological Survey estimates that a fluffy, ordinary cumulus cloud holds roughly 500 tonnes of water, about the weight of a hundred elephants. It floats because that water is spread out as countless tiny droplets in a huge volume of slightly warmer, rising air.
items.q: Roughly how much water does a typical cumulus cloud hold?
items.a: About 500 tonnes, roughly a hundred elephants' worth.

items.title: Firouzja wins Titled Tuesday on 10/11
items.body: Alireza Firouzja won the 3 November Titled Tuesday outright and unbeaten with 10/11, with Hikaru Nakamura second on 9.5/11. Eight players, including Nakamura, Firouzja and Wesley So, have now qualified for the Speed Chess Championship through their Titled Tuesday results.

items.title: Words plus pictures
items.body: Dual coding is the idea that we remember better when an idea arrives both as words and as an image. Sketch a quick box-and-arrow diagram next to your notes, and you give your memory two doors into the same room instead of one. The drawing doesn't need to be good, only yours.
items.hook: Wonder: what would today's hardest idea look like as three boxes and two arrows?

items.title: Pressure cooker, 7 am
items.body:
Three whistles from the kitchen,
each one a little louder,
like someone counting
slowly to wake the house.

By the third,
the dal is soft,
the window fogged,
and everyone is up.

items.title: StateBench: remembering a fact vs. keeping track
items.body: Ai2 has released StateBench, a benchmark that separates looking up a fixed fact from following a value as it changes step by step. Its matched tasks climb through four levels, and Ai2 reports frontier models drop to 13% accuracy or lower on the longest, hardest ones. Code and data are open.
items.q: What skill does StateBench separate from simple fact retrieval?
items.a: State tracking: following values as they are updated step by step.

items.title: Rubin spots two more of the Milky Way's quiet companions
items.body: The Vera C. Rubin Observatory has picked out two more faint satellites of our galaxy: one an ultra-faint dwarf galaxy, the other a globular cluster. Each is a small leftover from the Milky Way's long history of gathering up smaller neighbours.
items.q: What two kinds of object did Rubin newly find around the Milky Way?
items.a: An ultra-faint dwarf galaxy and a globular cluster.

items.title: Earth is closest to the Sun in January
items.body: Earth's orbit is slightly elliptical, and it reaches perihelion, its closest point to the Sun, in early January. Seasons come from the tilt of Earth's axis, not from distance, which is why January is winter in the north and summer in the south.
items.q: Do seasons come from Earth's distance to the Sun?
items.a: No. They come from the tilt of Earth's axis; Earth is actually closest to the Sun in early January.

items.body: Whatever you hear, and from whomever you hear it, wisdom is seeing the truth within it.

items.title: Bus stop, after rain
items.body:
The puddle holds
a whole streetlight,
quietly,
like a coin it found.

The bus comes.
The light shivers,
settles,
keeps it anyway.

items.title: Desirable difficulties
items.body: Robert and Elizabeth Bjork coined 'desirable difficulties' for learning conditions that feel harder in the moment but improve long-term memory: spacing practice out, mixing problem types, testing yourself instead of rereading. The struggle is not a sign it isn't working; often it is the work.
