items.title: Linux began as a hobby
items.body: On 25 August 1991, a Finnish student named Linus Torvalds posted to a Usenet newsgroup that he was writing a free operating system for 386 PCs, just as a hobby, and asked what features people would like. That modest post grew into the kernel that now runs most of the world's servers and every Android phone.
items.hook: Wonder: which of today's small hobby projects will quietly become infrastructure?

items.title: equals and hashCode travel together
items.body: In Java, if two objects are equal by equals(), they must return the same hashCode(). Override one without the other and a HashMap or HashSet may file equal objects in different buckets, so lookups quietly fail. Records generate both for you, consistently.
items.q: If a.equals(b) is true, what must be true of their hash codes?
items.a: a.hashCode() must equal b.hashCode().

items.title: The farthest point from Earth's centre
items.body: Everest is the highest peak above sea level, but the summit of Chimborazo in Ecuador is the point on Earth's surface farthest from the planet's centre. Earth bulges at the equator, and Chimborazo sits almost on it.
items.hook: Wonder: what else changes when you measure from the centre instead of the surface?

items.title: OpenAI builds its own Git backend
items.body: OpenAI says it built Pando, a Git-compatible backend, to keep up with the volume of code changes from engineers and coding agents. It now hosts the company's main repository, cut median push latency by almost 80 per cent, and serves close to a petabyte of repository data each day.
items.q: What is Pando?
items.a: A Git-compatible backend OpenAI built to handle code changes from engineers and coding agents.

items.title: Let the character want something small
items.body: A character doesn't need to want to save the world. A seat by the window, the last mango, one more minute before the alarm. A small, clear want on the first page gives readers something to lean toward, and it reveals personality in how the character goes after it.

items.title: A chess problem-solving final comes to Fujairah
items.body: The Grand Final of the WFCC Fujairah Grand Prix will be held in Fujairah, UAE, from 27 to 30 November. Solvers race through six rounds of composed problems and studies, and a composing contest runs alongside, with the solvers voting for their favourite original creations.
items.hook: Wonder: is solving a composed puzzle closer to playing chess or to reading poetry?

items.title: Kailasanathar Temple, Kanchipuram
items.body: The Kailasanathar Temple in Kanchipuram was built around 700 CE under the Pallava king Narasimhavarman II, also called Rajasimha. It is one of the earliest structural stone temples in Tamil Nadu, built of sandstone rather than cut into rock, and its walls are lined with small shrines and carvings.
items.q: Which Pallava king built the Kailasanathar Temple in Kanchipuram?
items.a: Narasimhavarman II (Rajasimha), around 700 CE.

items.title: One place, one kind of work
items.body: Brains link places with habits. If you can, give each kind of task its own spot: deep study at the desk, email on the sofa, reading by the window. Over time, simply sitting down in the study chair starts to switch the right mode on, with less willpower needed.

items.title: A model Earth with no life on it
items.body: Researchers have built a computer model of a lifeless Earth that links the atmosphere to the planet's interior. It can reproduce today's habitable-looking conditions without any life at all, a useful reminder for future exoplanet hunters that 'habitable' and 'inhabited' are different words.
items.hook: Wonder: what signal would truly convince you a distant world is alive?

items.title: If-then plans
items.body: Psychologist Peter Gollwitzer studied 'implementation intentions': plans phrased as 'If situation X, then I will do Y'. For example, 'If I sit down after dinner, then I open the Java notes first.' Linking an action to a cue makes it more likely to happen, because the cue does the remembering for you.
items.q: What is the format of an implementation intention?
items.a: 'If situation X, then I will do Y.'

items.title: Cache-aside, the polite cache
items.body: In the cache-aside pattern, the application checks the cache first. On a miss it reads the database, stores the result in the cache with a time-to-live, and returns it. On writes it updates the database and deletes the cached entry, rather than trying to update it, so the next read refills it fresh. Simple, common, and easy to reason about.
items.hook: Wonder: why is deleting a cache entry on write usually safer than updating it?

items.title: AI agents help run a radio telescope
items.body: At SETI's Allen Telescope Array, AI agents now assist with telescope operations and signal analysis. Researchers say some jobs dropped from weeks to hours, and the system detected a pulsar in the Crab Nebula in real time, a familiar natural lighthouse rather than anything alien.
items.q: What did the agent-assisted Allen Telescope Array detect in real time?
items.a: A pulsar in the Crab Nebula.

items.title: The tailor's measuring tape
items.body: For forty years the tailor wrote every customer's measurements in a ledger. When his granddaughter took over the shop, she found the margins full of tiny notes: 'stands straighter on Fridays', 'laughs with his whole chest, add room'. She bought a new ledger, kept the old one on the shelf, and on the first page of the new one she drew a wide, empty margin.

items.title: Young players gather in Al Ain
items.body: The fourth FIDE World Junior Rapid & Blitz Championships are under way in Al Ain, UAE, from 1 to 7 November, with 150 players from 40 countries. The nine-round rapid section finishes first, and blitz follows on 5–6 November. After three rounds, five players shared the Open lead on a perfect score.

items.title: Hummingbirds can fly backwards
items.body: Hummingbirds rotate their wings in a figure-eight pattern, producing lift on both the forward and back strokes. That lets them hover in place and even fly backwards, something almost no other bird can do.
items.q: What wing motion lets hummingbirds hover and fly backwards?
items.a: A figure-eight stroke that makes lift on both forward and back strokes.

items.body: Waste no more time arguing about what a good man should be. Be one.

items.title: The internet's first word was 'LO'
items.body: On 29 October 1969, a student at UCLA tried to log in to a computer at the Stanford Research Institute over the young ARPANET. He typed L, then O, and the system crashed before the G. So the first message ever sent across the network that grew into the internet was, fittingly, 'LO'. A full login worked about an hour later.
items.q: What were the first two letters sent over ARPANET?
items.a: L and O; the system crashed before 'LOGIN' was finished.

items.title: The sky Van Gogh actually saw
items.body: A study in Scientific Reports argues that the sky in The Starry Night matches the pre-dawn view over Saint-Rémy around 22 July 1889, when a waning crescent Moon, Venus and the Hyades star cluster sat close together. The painting may be more of a sky diary than we assumed.
items.hook: Wonder: which of your own skies would you want someone to identify 137 years later?

items.title: Attention residue
items.body: When you switch from task A to task B, part of your mind stays behind on A, especially if A was left unfinished. Researcher Sophie Leroy named this 'attention residue' in 2009. A small fix: before switching, jot where you stopped and what comes next. It gives A a resting place so B gets more of you.
items.q: What did Sophie Leroy call the leftover focus that lingers on a previous task?
items.a: Attention residue.

items.title: FlashProve: proof of which model answered
items.body: Anthropic, with collaborators from EPFL and MIT, has published FlashProve, an experimental system that attaches a cryptographic proof to a model's output showing it came from a specific, committed set of weights, without revealing the weights. It is released as research and code; no production deployment has been announced.
items.hook: Wonder: could a model's answer one day come with a receipt, like a signed letter?

items.title: Akam and puram: the two rooms of Sangam poetry
items.body: Classical Sangam poems in Tamil are sorted into two great modes. Akam ('inner') poems explore love and private feeling, usually without naming the people involved. Puram ('outer') poems speak of public life: kings, generosity, valour and ethics. Landscapes such as hills, seashore and farmland carry the mood of akam poems.
items.q: In Sangam poetry, which mode deals with love and inner feeling?
items.a: Akam ('inner').

items.title: Give stray thoughts a parking spot
items.body: Keep one notepad (or one notes file) beside you while you work. When a 'must remember to…' thought arrives, write five words and go back. The brain lets go more easily once it trusts the thought is caught somewhere safe. Review the pad when the session ends, not during it.

items.title: Java Strings never change, and that's the gift
items.body: A Java String is immutable: methods like toUpperCase() return a new String and leave the old one untouched. That makes Strings safe to share between threads, safe to use as HashMap keys, and lets the JVM pool identical literals. The cost: building text in a loop with + creates many throwaway objects, which is why StringBuilder exists.
items.q: Why use StringBuilder instead of + inside a long loop?
items.a: Strings are immutable, so each + creates a new object; StringBuilder appends into one mutable buffer.

items.title: World Senior Championship opens in Serbia
items.body: The FIDE World Senior Championship has begun in Vrnjačka Banja, Serbia, with 385 players from 65 federations, including 44 grandmasters. Four nine-round Swiss sections run in parallel: Open and Women, each for players over 50 and over 65, all at a classical time control.
items.hook: Wonder: what does a game look like after fifty years of pattern-building?

items.title: Rangoli at dusk
items.body:
She bends to the threshold
with a pinch of white,
and the dots wait patiently
to be joined into light.

By morning the feet
will have blurred every line.
She knows. She draws anyway.
That is the design.

items.title: Apple opens Siri to app developers
items.body: Apple has started a developer preview that lets apps plug their content and actions into Siri through App Intents, in the iOS 27.3 and sibling betas. Apps can offer multi-step 'Skills', such as checking an order and then arranging its delivery. Wider availability is planned later.
items.q: Which Apple framework lets apps expose actions to Siri?
items.a: App Intents.

items.title: All five genetic letters found in asteroid Ryugu
items.body: A Japanese team reports in Nature Astronomy that samples of asteroid Ryugu, brought home by JAXA's Hayabusa2 in 2020, contain all five nucleobases used in DNA and RNA: adenine, guanine, cytosine, thymine and uracil, in broadly similar amounts. It hints that these building blocks were common across the young Solar System.
items.hook: Wonder: how many of life's ingredients were already drifting around before Earth existed?

items.title: Koalas have fingerprints
items.body: Koalas have fingerprints with loops and whorls so similar to ours that they can be hard to tell apart even under a microscope. They evolved separately, probably to help grip branches and handle leaves.

items.title: Give your agent a budget
items.body: A good agent loop has limits: maximum steps, maximum tool calls, maximum time or tokens. When the budget runs out, it stops and reports what it has, instead of wandering. Budgets turn 'it went quiet for an hour' into 'here's where I got to'.
items.hook: Wonder: what budget would you give yourself for today's hardest task?

items.title: Leave the last step to the reader
items.body: Don't write 'she was heartbroken'. Write that she set two cups on the table, then put one back. Readers love to complete the thought themselves; the feeling they work out lands deeper than the one you hand them.

items.title: Ask 'why would that be true?'
items.body: When you read a fact, pause and ask why it makes sense, and answer in a sentence. This 'elaborative interrogation' ties new information to what you already know, and studies find it helps facts stick better than rereading.
items.q: What is elaborative interrogation?
items.a: Asking yourself why a fact is true and explaining it, to link it to what you already know.

items.title: Speed Chess Championship XI announced
items.body: Chess.com announced the 11th Speed Chess Championship, its 10th-anniversary edition, with a $250,000 prize fund and live finals in London.

items.title: The outbox pattern
items.body: You need to save an order AND publish an 'order created' event. Doing both separately risks one succeeding and one failing. Instead, write the event into an 'outbox' table inside the same database transaction as the order. A separate relay reads the outbox and publishes. Either both are recorded, or neither.
items.q: What problem does the outbox pattern solve?
items.a: Keeping a database write and an event publish consistent without a distributed transaction.

items.title: As deep as the water
items.body:
The lotus stem rises as high as the water is deep;
a person rises as high as the depth within.

items.title: Cut, copy, paste came from Xerox PARC
items.body: Larry Tesler and Tim Mott built the Gypsy text editor at Xerox PARC in the mid-1970s, which popularised cut, copy and paste with a mouse. Tesler championed 'modeless' editing, where every key does the same thing no matter what mode you're in.
items.hook: Wonder: how many times did you paste something today?

items.title: The Moon is drifting away, slowly
items.body: Laser beams bounced off mirrors left by Apollo astronauts show the Moon moving away from Earth by about 3.8 cm a year, roughly the speed your fingernails grow. Tides are the cause: they slowly pass Earth's spin energy to the Moon's orbit.
items.q: How fast is the Moon receding from Earth?
items.a: About 3.8 cm per year.

items.title: Anthropic's Message Threads skip the resend
items.body: A new public-beta API feature lets developers send a long conversation once, then only the new messages plus a thread ID. Anthropic says this cuts median time-to-first-token by about a third on very long requests.

items.title: Uthiramerur's palm-leaf pot
items.body: Inscriptions on a temple wall at Uthiramerur, near Kanchipuram, dated to the reign of Parantaka Chola I (around 920 CE), describe how a village chose its committee members: names written on palm leaves were dropped into a pot, and a child drew them out. The rules also listed who was eligible to stand.
items.q: In the Uthiramerur system, who drew the palm-leaf names from the pot?
items.a: A young child.

items.title: Ceiling fan
items.body:
Slow circles above the bed,
like someone stirring the room
until the day dissolves.

items.title: Decide once, then stop deciding
items.body: Small decisions quietly drain the tank. Pick defaults for the repeat ones: the same breakfast on weekdays, a go-to lunch order, a fixed 'laundry day'. A default isn't a rule; you can break it any time. It just means the easy path is already chosen.

items.title: IceCube catches very high-energy neutrinos
items.body: The IceCube detector, a cubic kilometre of Antarctic ice laced with sensors, is recording neutrinos carrying roughly ten billion times the energy of those from the Sun, messengers from far-off cosmic engines.
items.q: Where is the IceCube neutrino detector?
items.a: Buried in the ice at the South Pole, Antarctica.

items.title: Walk, then brainstorm
items.body: In Stanford experiments by Marily Oppezzo and Daniel Schwartz (2014), people came up with noticeably more creative uses for everyday objects while walking, even on a treadmill facing a blank wall, than while sitting. The boost lingered a little after they sat down.
items.hook: Wonder: what problem could you take on a ten-minute walk today?

items.title: Java Optional: a return type, not a field
items.body: Optional was designed to say 'this method might not have an answer'. Return it from finders; don't use it for fields, method parameters or collections (return an empty list instead). And prefer orElseGet(() -> expensive()) over orElse(expensive()) when the fallback is costly, because orElse always evaluates its argument.
items.q: Why prefer orElseGet over orElse for an expensive fallback?
items.a: orElse evaluates its argument every time; orElseGet only calls the supplier when the Optional is empty.

items.title: Gawain Jones takes the English title
items.body: Gawain Maroroa Jones won the 2026 English Championship unbeaten with 7.5/9, a full point ahead of Michael Adams. Elmira Mirzoeva won the women's title.

items.title: The night watchman of the bakery
items.body: Every night at three, Ravi unlocked the bakery and switched on one lamp, not to work, just to listen. The dough rose in its tins with tiny sighs. He'd been a watchman for thirty years and this was the only building that seemed to breathe back. At five the bakers came, loud and floury. He handed them the keys and the quiet, and walked home with a warm bun in his pocket that nobody ever charged him for.

items.title: Butterflies taste with their feet
items.body: Butterflies have taste sensors on their feet. When a female lands on a leaf, she can 'taste' it to check that it's the right plant for her caterpillars before laying eggs.
items.q: Why does a butterfly taste a leaf with its feet?
items.a: To check it's the right food plant for its caterpillars before laying eggs.

items.title: Meituan releases LongCat-2.5
items.body: Meituan launched LongCat-2.5, a large multimodal model aimed at long coding sessions and visual understanding. It is a mixture-of-experts design: only a small slice of its parameters wakes up for each token.
items.hook: Wonder: why might waking only part of a model per word save so much energy?

items.title: The smiley was born on a bulletin board
items.body: On 19 September 1982, Carnegie Mellon professor Scott Fahlman suggested typing :-) to mark jokes on the department's online bulletin board, and :-( for serious posts. It spread from there to the whole internet.
items.q: Who proposed the :-) emoticon, and where?
items.a: Scott Fahlman, on a Carnegie Mellon bulletin board in 1982.

items.title: The world is change
items.body: The universe is change; our life is what our thoughts make it.

items.title: Hera gets its first clear look at Didymos and Dimorphos
items.body: ESA's Hera spacecraft has taken its first clear view of the asteroid pair that NASA's DART probe nudged in 2022. Hera is now closing in to map how the small moonlet was reshaped.
items.q: What did DART do to the asteroid Dimorphos in 2022?
items.a: It deliberately struck it to test whether an asteroid's path can be nudged.

items.title: Delhi's iron pillar that rarely rusts
items.body: The iron pillar now in Delhi's Qutb complex is about 1,600 years old, from the Gupta era, and still shows remarkably little rust. Metallurgists credit iron rich in phosphorus, which helps a thin, protective film form on the surface over time.
items.hook: Wonder: what would a 1,600-year-old object of yours look like?

items.title: Chunking: why masters see more
items.body: In classic studies, strong chess players glanced at a real game position for a few seconds and rebuilt it far better than novices, but the advantage almost vanished for randomly scattered pieces. Experts don't have bigger memories; they store familiar patterns as single chunks.
items.q: Why did experts' memory advantage shrink with random chess positions?
items.a: Random positions have no familiar patterns to chunk, so experts lose their shortcut.

items.title: Give your keys a home port
items.body: Choose one spot by the door, a bowl or hook, for keys, wallet, earphones and badge. Things that leave the house only come back to that spot. You're not relying on remembering; you're relying on the place. Put tomorrow's must-carry item there tonight.

items.title: Token bucket: rate limiting with a jar of coins
items.body: Picture a jar that refills with one coin every 100 ms, up to a cap of 20. Each request spends a coin; an empty jar means 'wait'. The cap allows short bursts, the refill rate sets the long-run speed. Store just two numbers per client: tokens left and last refill time, and top up lazily when a request arrives.
items.q: In a token bucket, what does the bucket's capacity control?
items.a: How big a burst is allowed; the refill rate controls the sustained rate.

items.title: Morning steel
items.body:
The tumbler on the counter
holds one stripe of sun,
like it was asked to carry it
and hasn't yet said no.

I drink around the light.
It stays.

items.title: Lazavik wins the KazChess Masters unbeaten
items.body: Nineteen-year-old Denis Lazavik won the KazChess Masters in Almaty with 6.5/9 and no losses, half a point ahead of Daniil Dubov. Fourteen-year-old IM Mark Smirnov tied for third and earned his first GM norm.
items.q: Which 14-year-old earned his first GM norm in Almaty?
items.a: IM Mark Smirnov of Kazakhstan.

items.title: OpenAI's LifeVal tests everyday chores
items.body: OpenAI published LifeVal, a benchmark built from time-use studies and a survey of nearly 4,000 people. Instead of exam puzzles, it asks whether AI can help with ordinary life tasks like planning a household budget or finding childcare.
items.hook: Wonder: which of your weekly chores would make a good benchmark question?

items.title: Voyager 1 nears one light-day from home
items.body: Launched in 1977, Voyager 1 is now approaching a full light-day from Earth: a radio message from mission control takes about 24 hours to reach it. Engineers keep it doing science with careful power-saving moves.
items.q: Roughly how long will a radio signal take to reach Voyager 1 once it is one light-day away?
items.a: About 24 hours.

items.title: Betelgeuse breathes slowly
items.body: Betelgeuse, the red shoulder of Orion, swells and dims in a rhythm of roughly 430 days, with a longer cycle of about six years on top. It is around 650 light-years away, so the light you see tonight set out around the 1300s, when the Vijayanagara Empire was young.
items.hook: Wonder: find Orion before dawn this week and compare Betelgeuse with orange Aldebaran nearby. Which looks brighter?

items.title: The short nap sweet spot
items.body: Naps of about 10 to 20 minutes tend to lift alertness without the groggy feeling that longer naps can bring, because you wake before sliding into deep sleep. Early afternoon, when energy naturally dips, is the usual best time.
items.q: Why do short naps avoid grogginess?
items.a: You wake before entering deep sleep, so there's little sleep inertia.

items.title: Filter coffee
items.body:
Decoction drips through the night,
patient as rain on a tin roof.

In the morning, poured high
from tumbler to dabara,
the froth rises like a small applause
for having waited.

items.title: A perfect 9/9 in Karnataka blitz
items.body: FM Aarav Sarbalia won the Karnataka State Blitz Championship in Tumkur on 1 November with a perfect 9 out of 9. A day earlier he had finished second in the state rapid championship with 8 out of 9. ChessBase India ran a warm piece about the weekend, written by his father.

items.title: Decide first
items.body: First say to yourself what you would be; and then do what you have to do.

items.title: Read replicas and the 'where did my write go?' moment
items.body: A read replica copies the main database a little behind. If a user saves a profile and the next page reads from a replica, they may see the old value. A common fix is read-your-writes: for a short time after someone writes, send their reads to the primary.
items.q: What is 'read-your-writes' consistency?
items.a: A guarantee that a user always sees their own recent writes, often by reading from the primary for a short time after writing.

items.title: Small galaxies let most of their oxygen go
items.body: A Hubble survey of 37 nearby dwarf galaxies found they kept only about 11% of the oxygen their stars ever made, on average. The rest was likely blown out by exploding stars, because small galaxies have too little gravity to hold on. The oxygen isn't lost to the universe; it now drifts in the space around them.
items.hook: Wonder: could some of the oxygen in our own bodies once have been blown out of a smaller galaxy?

items.title: Give transitions a soft landing
items.body: Switching tasks is often the hardest part. Set a gentle five-minute warning before you need to stop, so the switch doesn't arrive as a jolt. Use the minutes to wind down: save, stretch, refill your water. The ending stops being a cliff and becomes a slope.

items.title: A hard drive that weighed a ton
items.body: IBM's first hard disk, the 350 RAMAC of 1956, stored about five million characters on fifty spinning platters 24 inches across. The whole unit weighed roughly a ton. Today a fingernail-sized card holds far, far more.
items.q: What year did IBM ship its first hard-disk system, the RAMAC?

items.title: Let an object hold the feeling
items.body: Instead of telling readers a character is lonely, show the second cup she still sets out each morning. Objects carry emotion without announcing it, and readers enjoy doing the last step of understanding themselves.
items.q: What does 'let an object hold the feeling' mean?
items.a: Show an emotion through a concrete thing a character uses or keeps, rather than naming the emotion.

items.title: The Eiffel Tower is taller in summer
items.body: Iron expands when it warms. On hot days the top of the Eiffel Tower can sit up to about 15 cm higher than on cold winter days, and it leans very slightly away from the sun as one side heats faster than the other.
items.hook: Wonder: what other everyday things quietly grow and shrink with the seasons?

items.title: Chola bronzes begin as wax
items.body: The famous Chola bronzes, like the dancing Nataraja, were made by the lost-wax method. The sculptor shapes the figure in wax, coats it in clay, heats it so the wax runs out, then pours molten metal into the hollow. Each mould is broken to free the statue, so every piece is one of a kind. Artisans in Swamimalai, near Kumbakonam, still work this way.
items.q: Why is every lost-wax bronze unique?
items.a: The clay mould is broken to release the casting, so it can be used only once.

items.title: Every agent needs a 'done' line
items.body: An agent loop keeps going until something tells it to stop. A good stop condition is concrete: tests pass, the file exists, the user confirmed, or ten steps have passed. Without one, an agent can polish forever or wander. Writing the finish line first is half the design.
items.hook: Wonder: what's the finish line for the task you're working on right now?

items.title: Doodling can help you listen
items.body: In a 2009 study by Jackie Andrade, people who shaded shapes while listening to a dull phone message later recalled about 29% more of it than people who just listened. A light doodle may keep the mind from wandering off entirely.
items.q: In Andrade's 2009 study, how much more did doodlers remember?
items.a: About 29% more.

items.title: The rule of the square
items.body: Can a lone king catch a passed pawn? Draw an imaginary square: one side runs from the pawn to its promotion square, and the square extends sideways toward the king. If the king can step into that square on its move, it catches the pawn. If not, the pawn runs home. No counting needed, just a glance.
items.hook: Wonder: why does a pawn on its starting rank need a slightly bigger square? (It can move two squares at once.)

items.title: Java try-with-resources: cleanup you can't forget
items.body:
Since Java 7, you can declare a resource inside try( ... ). When the block ends, normally or with an exception, Java calls close() on it for you, in reverse order of opening. It works with anything that implements AutoCloseable: files, sockets, database connections.

try (var in = Files.newBufferedReader(path)) { ... }
items.q: Which interface must a class implement to be used in try-with-resources?
items.a: AutoCloseable (Closeable extends it).

items.title: The repair shop's waiting chair
items.body: Mr. Iyer fixed radios that nobody needed anymore. People brought them anyway, and while he worked they sat in the single wooden chair by the door. He never hurried. One afternoon a girl asked why. He turned the dial until a station bloomed out of the hiss. 'Because,' he said, 'the waiting is part of what I'm giving back.'

items.title: Perseverance becomes the farthest-driving vehicle on another world
items.body: NASA's Perseverance rover has now driven 45.22 km (28.10 miles) on Mars, more than any vehicle has ever driven beyond Earth. It reached the mark on 11 October 2026, and Guinness presented a plaque to its engineering twin back on Earth. The rover can now also work out its position on its own by matching what it sees to orbital maps.
items.q: How far has Perseverance driven on Mars?
items.a: 45.22 km (28.10 miles), a record for any vehicle on another world.

items.title: No longer talk about it
items.body: No longer talk at all about the kind of man that a good man ought to be, but be such.

items.title: Copilot gets 'connect once' tools
items.body: GitHub has added connectors in preview that let Copilot reach about 26 services, including Slack, Figma, Notion and Linear. You sign in once and the connection works across the command line, the editor, mobile and the cloud. Less setup, more of the agent's time spent on the actual work.

items.title: Sea otters hold hands while they sleep
items.body: Sea otters often sleep floating on their backs, and some hold paws or wrap themselves in kelp so they don't drift apart from each other. A floating group of resting otters is called a raft.
items.q: What is a floating group of sea otters called?
items.a: A raft.

items.title: The first mouse wore wood
items.body: The first computer mouse, built in 1964 by Bill English from Douglas Engelbart's design, was a small wooden block with two metal wheels underneath and a single button on top. One wheel tracked left-right, the other up-down.
items.hook: Wonder: why did it get called a 'mouse'? (The cord looked like a tail.)

items.title: Bundle the dull with the delightful
items.body: Save something you enjoy, like a favourite podcast or audiobook, only for a task you tend to avoid: laundry, dishes, expense reports. A 2014 study found people went to the gym more when their gripping audiobooks were only available there. The boring task becomes the doorway to the good thing.
items.q: What is 'temptation bundling'?
items.a: Pairing a treat you want with a task you avoid, and allowing the treat only during that task.

items.title: The man who taught us to read Ashoka again
items.body: For centuries, nobody could read the Brahmi script on Ashoka's pillars and rocks. In 1837, James Prinsep, working in Calcutta, cracked it, helped by short donor inscriptions at Sanchi that repeated the same word endings. Suddenly an emperor's messages from the 3rd century BCE could speak again.
items.hook: Wonder: which script used in India today descends from Brahmi? (Nearly all of them do, Tamil included.)

items.title: Bloom filters: a polite 'probably'
items.body: A Bloom filter is a tiny bit array plus a few hash functions. To add an item, you set the bits its hashes point to. To check an item, you look at those bits: if any is 0, the item is definitely not there; if all are 1, it is probably there. Databases use them to skip disk reads for keys that can't exist.
items.q: Can a Bloom filter give a false negative?
items.a: No. It can give false positives ('probably there') but never false negatives.

items.title: Guess first, learn better
items.body: Trying to answer a question before you've learned the material, even when you get it wrong, tends to improve how well you remember the right answer afterwards. Researchers call this the pretesting effect. The guess seems to open a slot in your mind that the real answer then fills.
items.q: What is the pretesting effect?
items.a: Attempting to answer before learning, even wrongly, improves later memory of the correct answer.

items.title: Firouzja wins the Bullet Brawl
items.body: Alireza Firouzja won Chess.com's Bullet Brawl arena on 31 October with 170 points, just ahead of Hikaru Nakamura on 166. Nakamura led into the final stretch, but Firouzja scored 13.5 out of 15 in the last quarter of the two-hour, one-minute-per-side event. The next Brawl is on 7 November.
items.hook: Wonder: what does a strong player still see in a one-minute game that the rest of us miss?

items.title: Night shift of the stars
items.body:
The city switches off its windows
one by one, like someone
putting books back on a shelf.

Up there, nobody clocks in.
The stars were already working
long before we needed light.

items.title: Rubin may have found a new dwarf planet beyond Pluto
items.body: The Vera Rubin Observatory has spotted a large icy world, provisionally called 2026 ED138, about 46 times farther from the Sun than Earth is. It is estimated at 600 to 1,500 km across and had been hiding against the crowded starfields of the Milky Way. If its size is confirmed, it could join Pluto, Ceres, Eris, Haumea and Makemake as a recognised dwarf planet.
items.q: Roughly how far from the Sun is 2026 ED138, in AU?
items.a: About 46 AU, beyond Pluto's average distance of about 40 AU.

items.title: Android Studio lets you bring your own coding agent
items.body: Android Studio's latest build lets developers pick from more than 40 coding agents and switch between them. They plug in through the open Agent Client Protocol, so an agent can see the project, run builds, and read the emulator's logs. The nice idea: the IDE becomes a shared workbench, and the agent is a swappable tool on it.
items.hook: Wonder: what would you want any coding agent to be able to see in your project, and what should stay off-limits?

items.body: Very little indeed is needed for living a happy life.

items.title: Honeybees dance directions
items.body: A forager bee that finds good flowers does a 'waggle dance' back in the hive. The angle of her waggle run, measured against straight up, matches the angle between the food and the Sun. How long she waggles tells the others how far away it is. Karl von Frisch shared a Nobel Prize in 1973 for working this out.
items.q: What does the length of a bee's waggle run communicate?
items.a: How far away the food source is.

items.title: Sleep files the day's learning
items.body: While you sleep, the brain replays and consolidates what you practised that day. That's why a skill can feel smoother the next morning even though you didn't practise overnight. A short review before bed, followed by a real night's sleep, is a quietly effective way to study.

items.title: Java sealed interfaces: a closed list of shapes
items.body: A sealed interface names exactly which classes may implement it, for example: sealed interface Shape permits Circle, Square. Combine that with records and pattern-matching switch, and the compiler can confirm you've handled every case. Leave one out and the code won't compile.
items.q: What does the 'permits' clause on a sealed interface do?
items.a: It lists the only classes allowed to implement it, which lets switches over it be checked for exhaustiveness.

items.body: Dig a well in sand and water rises; learn, and wisdom rises the same way, the deeper you go.

items.title: Sunlight is about eight minutes old
items.body: On average, light from the Sun takes about 8 minutes and 20 seconds to reach Earth. Light from the Moon takes a little over a second. When you watch a sunrise, you're seeing the Sun as it was eight minutes earlier.
items.q: How long does sunlight take to reach Earth, on average?
items.a: About 8 minutes 20 seconds.

items.title: Specific beats general
items.body: 'She brought food' slides right past the reader. 'She brought rasam in a steel tiffin, still warm' lands, because one concrete detail does the work of a paragraph of explaining. When a sentence feels flat, ask what someone would actually see, smell or hold.

items.title: C was made to rewrite an operating system
items.body: Around 1972 at Bell Labs, Dennis Ritchie created the C language, growing it out of an earlier language called B. In 1973 most of Unix was rewritten in C. That made it much easier to move the system to new hardware, and many operating systems and languages since then descend from that choice.
items.q: Which operating system was largely rewritten in C in 1973?
items.a: Unix.

items.title: Name the next action as a verb
items.body: 'Taxes' is a cloud. 'Open the bank app and download the October statement' is a step you can take. When a task feels heavy, rewrite it until it starts with a physical verb you could do in five minutes.

items.title: Triangulation: losing a move on purpose
items.body: In some king-and-pawn endings, the side to move is the one in trouble. A king can walk around a small triangle of three squares and come back to where it started, using up one tempo. The opponent's king, short on room, can't copy the manoeuvre. Now it's their move, and the position works in your favour.
items.q: What does triangulation achieve in an endgame?
items.a: It passes the obligation to move to the opponent by losing a tempo with the king.

items.title: A flamboyance of flamingos
items.body: A group of flamingos is called a flamboyance. Their pink colour comes from pigments called carotenoids in the algae and small shrimp they eat. A flamingo chick hatches grey-white and turns pink gradually as it grows.
items.hook: Wonder: what would your own collective noun be?

items.title: A tool description is a prompt
items.body: When an agent picks a tool, mostly what it has to go on is the tool's name and its short description. A vague description gets used in vague ways. Write each one like a note to a smart new colleague: what the tool does, when to use it, when not to, and what it returns.

items.title: The Shore Temple at Mamallapuram
items.body: The Shore Temple has stood beside the Bay of Bengal for about 1,300 years. It was built under the Pallava king Narasimhavarman II, also called Rajasimha, around the early 8th century. It's one of the earliest structural stone temples in South India, built from cut blocks of granite rather than carved out of a single rock.
items.q: Which dynasty built the Shore Temple at Mamallapuram?
items.a: The Pallavas, under Narasimhavarman II (Rajasimha).

items.title: Explain it to an empty chair
items.body: Say a new idea out loud, as if you're teaching it to someone who isn't there. The places where you stumble are exactly the gaps in your understanding. This is the self-explanation effect, and it's one of the cheaper study habits that has been well studied.

items.title: Write-ahead logs: write down the plan, then act
items.body: Before a database changes its data files, it first appends a description of the change to a sequential log and makes sure that log is safely on disk. If the machine crashes partway through, replaying the log on restart brings everything back to a consistent state. Appending to a log is fast, and it turns 'what was I doing?' into a solved problem.
items.q: Why does a database write to its WAL before the data files?
items.a: So that after a crash it can replay the log and reach a consistent state.

items.title: The bookbinder's spare thread
items.body: Every evening the old bookbinder cut one extra length of thread and left it on the windowsill. 'For the book I haven't been given yet,' she would say. Years later, a girl brought her a notebook falling apart, full of a grandmother's recipes. The thread was waiting. It was exactly long enough.

items.title: Chess.com Crazyhouse Championship starts 5 November
items.body: In crazyhouse, a piece you capture changes sides and can be dropped back onto the board as your own. Chess.com's 2026 Crazyhouse Championship begins with 3+0 qualifying arenas on 5 November. Each arena winner goes through to an eight-player double-elimination final on 6 November. The prize fund is $2,500.
items.hook: Wonder: how would your openings change if captured pieces came back to fight for you?

items.title: Saturn's rings are astonishingly thin
items.body: Saturn's main rings are about 280,000 km across, yet in most places they're only tens of metres thick. If you shrank them to the width of a football field, they'd be much thinner than a sheet of paper. When Earth lines up edge-on with them, they nearly vanish from view.
items.q: Roughly how thick are Saturn's main rings in most places?
items.a: Only about tens of metres, even though they span about 280,000 km.

items.body: While we are postponing, life speeds by.

items.title: Karpathy builds a calm video library in one morning
items.body: Andrej Karpathy used AI coding help to turn about 20 years of Hacker News video recommendations into a browsable site called HackerTube, and reportedly did it in a single morning. The finished site is just a quiet curated directory with no chatbot in it. The AI did the building and then stepped out of the way.
items.hook: Wonder: what old pile of bookmarks of yours could become a little library?

items.title: The first website is still online
items.body: Tim Berners-Lee published the first website at CERN in 1991. It explained what the World Wide Web was and how to use it. CERN later put a restored copy back up at its original address, info.cern.ch, so you can still read it.
items.q: At which lab was the first website published?
items.a: CERN, in 1991.

items.title: Keep a 'done list' next to the to-do list
items.body: At the end of the day, write down three things you actually finished, small ones included. A to-do list only ever shows what's missing. A done list gives you proof that you moved, and that makes tomorrow's start easier.

items.title: Keezhadi: a Sangam-age town by the Vaigai
items.body: Near Madurai, excavations at Keezhadi have turned up an ancient urban settlement: brick buildings, drains, wells, beads, dice and pottery. Some of the pots carry Tamil-Brahmi letters. Taken together, the finds suggest literacy was quite widespread in early Tamil country.
items.q: What script appears on pottery at Keezhadi?
items.a: Tamil-Brahmi.

items.title: Scotland's national animal is a unicorn
items.body: The unicorn has been a Scottish heraldic symbol since at least the 15th century. You can see it on the royal coat of arms used in Scotland. It stood for purity and strength, and in legend it could only be tamed by someone pure of heart.
items.hook: Wonder: what animal would you pick to stand for your own household?

items.title: Circuit breakers: stop knocking on a closed door
items.body: Once calls to a dependency start failing over and over, a circuit breaker 'opens' and fails fast for a while instead of piling up waiting requests. After a cool-down it goes 'half-open' and lets one trial call through. A success closes it again. A failure keeps it open. The point is that the struggling service gets room to recover.
items.q: What are the three states of a circuit breaker?
items.a: Closed (normal), open (fail fast) and half-open (let a trial call through).

items.title: The spacing effect: let it fade a little
items.body: Reviewing something just as it starts to slip makes the memory stronger than reviewing it while it still feels fresh. A small struggle to recall tells the brain the thing is worth keeping. A workable rhythm: look again after a day, then three days, then a week.
items.q: Why does spaced review beat cramming?
items.a: Recalling something as it begins to fade strengthens the memory more than re-reading it while it's still fresh.

items.title: Sindarov comes back to win Clutch Chess in Saint Louis
items.body: Javokhir Sindarov won the 2026 Clutch Chess: Champions Showdown with 20.5 points, after starting the final day 2½ points behind. Praggnanandhaa took second place, 1½ points back. Nakamura and Caruana made up the four-player field. The event ran from 27 to 29 October.
items.q: Who came second at the 2026 Clutch Chess Champions Showdown?
items.a: Praggnanandhaa, 1½ points behind Sindarov.

items.title: First light
items.body:
The milk van hums its single note,
the neem tree shakes the dark off slowly.
No one has asked anything of you yet.
Sit inside that for a minute.
It is the softest room in the house.

items.title: Webb finds the interstellar comet's ice is unusual
items.body: JWST looked at the interstellar comet 3I/ATLAS three times, starting in August 2025 and ending after its closest pass by the Sun. One water-ice signal stayed strong while two others hardly showed. The team's reading is that the ice comes as very fine, dusty grains, more like some distant objects beyond Neptune than like familiar comets. The study appeared in The Astrophysical Journal Letters.
items.q: Which part of our solar system did 3I/ATLAS's ice most resemble?
items.a: Some trans-Neptunian objects, the small icy bodies beyond Neptune.

items.title: DeepSeek shares a prototype coding agent that doesn't wait to be asked
items.body: DeepSeek has shown a 'Super-Agent' for coding that offers fixes on its own initiative instead of waiting for a prompt. The code is up on GitHub as an open-source research prototype. DeepSeek says plainly that it isn't a finished product yet.
items.hook: Wonder: when should a helper speak up, and when should it stay quiet?

items.title: Late tram
items.body:
Half the seats are sleeping,
the other half are me.
The city passes softly,
lit like a slow sea.

I do not need to be anywhere
faster than this light.
The stops say their own names aloud
and hand me to the night.

items.title: Consistent hashing in one breath
items.body: With plain hash(key) mod N, adding one server reshuffles almost every key. Consistent hashing places both servers and keys on a ring and assigns each key to the next server clockwise. Add or remove a server and only about 1/N of the keys move. Virtual nodes (many points per server) smooth out the load.
items.q: Roughly what fraction of keys move when you add a server under consistent hashing?
items.a: About 1/N, versus nearly all keys with plain mod-N hashing.

items.title: Total Chess pilot opens in Budapest on 10 November
items.body: Norway Chess's FIDE-approved Total Chess event runs from 10 to 20 November at the Anantara New York Palace in Budapest. It combines three time controls: Fast Classic (45 minutes + 30 seconds), rapid and blitz. Twenty-four players, including Carlsen, Caruana, Praggnanandhaa, Arjun Erigaisi and Vaishali Rameshbabu, start with a blitz Swiss, then groups and knockouts. It pilots a full tour starting in March 2027.

items.title: Enter late, leave early
items.body: A screenwriting rule that works for any story: start a scene as late as possible and leave as soon as its point has landed. Skip the hellos and the walking in; open on the moment something shifts. Readers fill in the rest, and they enjoy doing it.
items.hook: Wonder: which sentence in your last piece is the real first sentence?

items.title: Olympus Mons, the gentle giant
items.body: Olympus Mons on Mars is the tallest volcano known in the solar system, rising about 22 km above its surroundings, roughly two and a half times Everest's height above sea level. Its slopes are so gentle that someone standing on it would barely notice the climb, and the summit would sit beyond the horizon.
items.q: Roughly how tall is Olympus Mons?
items.a: About 22 km, around 2.5 times Everest's height above sea level.

items.body: To speak harsh words when sweet ones are at hand is like plucking unripe fruit when the ripe is there for the taking.

items.title: The Mother of All Demos
items.body: On 9 December 1968 in San Francisco, Douglas Engelbart and his team showed the world a computer mouse, hypertext links, windowed views, collaborative real-time editing and video conferencing, all in one 90-minute presentation. Much of modern computing was previewed in that single afternoon.
items.q: Who gave the 1968 'Mother of All Demos' that introduced the mouse?
items.a: Douglas Engelbart.

items.title: Make the first step embarrassingly small
items.body: If a task won't start, shrink the first step until it feels almost silly: open the file; put on one shoe; write a single sentence. Starting is the bottleneck, and momentum usually does the rest. If it doesn't, that's fine too: you still moved, and that counts.

items.title: Wombats make cube-shaped droppings
items.body: Wombats are the only animals known to produce cube-shaped poo. A 2018 study found that the final stretch of their intestine has walls with varying stiffness that shape the droppings into cubes. Wombats stack them on rocks and logs as territorial markers, and the flat sides help them stay put.
items.hook: Wonder: what other shapes could nature 'manufacture' without any moulds?

items.title: Context compaction, the agent's tidy desk
items.body: Long-running agents fill their context window with old tool outputs and chatter. Compaction replaces older turns with a short summary while keeping recent turns verbatim. It's a trade: you keep the thread of the work and free space, but anything the summary leaves out is gone. Good compaction keeps decisions, open questions and file paths; it drops raw logs.
items.hook: Wonder: if you summarised your own workday in five lines, what would you be sure to keep?

items.title: Nalanda, the great monastery-university
items.body: Nalanda in present-day Bihar grew into a famous centre of learning from about the 5th century CE, under Gupta patronage. Students came from across Asia; the Chinese pilgrim-scholar Xuanzang studied there in the 7th century and wrote about its scholars and libraries. Its ruins are now a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
items.q: Which Chinese scholar studied at Nalanda in the 7th century?
items.a: Xuanzang.

items.title: The generation effect
items.body: You remember information better when you produce it yourself than when you simply read it. Slamecka and Graf described this in 1978: completing 'hot: c___' (cold) sticks better than reading 'hot: cold'. A cheap way to use it: before re-reading notes, try to write the key point from memory first.
items.hook: Wonder: what could you try to recall right now, before looking it up?

items.title: Java records: data, said plainly
items.body: Records, final since Java 16 (JEP 395), are a compact way to declare a class that is just data: record Point(int x, int y) {}. The compiler supplies the constructor, accessors x() and y(), equals, hashCode and toString. Fields are final, so records are shallowly immutable, which makes them ideal for DTOs, map keys and values passed between threads.
items.q: Which methods does the compiler generate for a Java record?
items.a: A canonical constructor, accessor methods, equals, hashCode and toString.

items.title: The opposition, in one picture
items.body: In king-and-pawn endings, two kings standing on the same file with one empty square between them are 'in opposition'. Whoever is NOT to move holds the opposition, because the other king must step aside and give ground. Many 'drawn or won?' pawn endings come down to this tiny standoff.
items.q: With kings facing each other one square apart, who has the opposition?
items.a: The side that is not to move.

items.title: The lending library of umbrellas
items.body: The bus stop had a bucket of umbrellas and a sign: Take one. Bring one back. Nobody knew who started it. Mira took a yellow one in June and forgot it for months. In October she returned it with a second umbrella, blue, that she'd bought on purpose. The next morning both were gone, and someone had left a third: green, with a note tied to the handle that said only, 'Your turn was lovely.'

items.title: Agents get their own identities in HashiCorp Vault
items.body: At IBM TechXchange on 27 October, IBM made HashiCorp Vault 2.2 with Agent Identity generally available, and previewed a new Secure Hub. The idea: each AI agent gets its own managed identity and short-lived credentials, rather than borrowing a human's keys. Integrations named include watsonx Orchestrate, Amazon Bedrock, Microsoft Foundry and Google Gemini.

items.title: Sharks are older than trees
items.body: Sharks appear in the fossil record around 450 million years ago. The earliest true trees came later, roughly 385 to 390 million years ago. So sharks were already swimming the seas before there were any forests on land.
items.q: Which came first, sharks or trees?
items.a: Sharks, by roughly 60 million years.

items.title: Hubble and Webb read the solar system's oldest postcards
items.body: Astronomers used Hubble and Webb together to study 27 small, distant objects beyond Neptune. These icy bodies have changed little since the solar system formed, so their surfaces act like a preserved record of the material the planets were built from.
items.hook: Wonder: what would a 4.5-billion-year-old snowball tell you about the day it formed?

items.title: Grace Hopper's nanosecond
items.body: To explain why satellite signals and fast computers were limited by distance, Grace Hopper handed out pieces of wire about 30 cm (11.8 inches) long: the distance light travels in one billionth of a second. She'd sometimes contrast it with a coil of wire representing a microsecond, nearly 300 metres long.
items.hook: Wonder: how far does light travel in the time your laptop finishes one clock cycle?

items.title: Interleaving: mix the practice
items.body: Practising one problem type in a block feels smooth, but mixing types (A, C, B, A, B, C) tends to produce better long-term results. Studies on maths learning, such as Rohrer and Taylor's, found that interleaved practice helps you learn to tell which method a problem needs, not just how to run the method. It feels harder while you do it, which is part of why it works.
items.q: Why does interleaved practice often beat blocked practice?
items.a: It trains you to recognise which strategy a problem needs, not just to execute one strategy repeatedly.

items.body: Nothing, Lucilius, is ours, except time.
items.who: Seneca, Letters to Lucilius, Letter I (tr. Gummere)

items.title: Leave a breadcrumb before you stop
items.body: Before you step away from a task, write one line: the very next physical action. Not 'finish the report', but 'open the draft and rewrite the second heading'. Restarting is often the hardest part with ADHD; a breadcrumb means future-you doesn't have to rebuild the whole mental map before taking the first step.

items.title: 1,330 couplets, built like a grid
items.body: Thiruvalluvar's Thirukkural is precisely structured: 133 chapters of 10 couplets each, 1,330 kurals in all. It is divided into three books: Aram (virtue), Porul (wealth and statecraft) and Inbam (love). Each kural is a two-line venba of seven metrical feet, four in the first line and three in the second.
items.q: How many chapters and couplets does the Thirukkural have?
items.a: 133 chapters of 10 couplets: 1,330 kurals, in three books (Aram, Porul, Inbam).

items.title: Backpressure: letting the slow part say 'not yet'
items.body: When a producer is faster than a consumer, something has to give. Without backpressure, queues grow until memory runs out. With it, the consumer signals how much it can take, and the producer slows down. Bounded queues that block, TCP's flow-control window, and Reactive Streams' request(n) are all the same idea: demand flows upstream, data flows downstream.
items.hook: Wonder: where in your system is an unbounded queue quietly waiting to become a memory problem?

items.title: Kettle
items.body:
The kettle hums its one long vowel,
the window fogs, then clears.
Nothing in this kitchen asks
for more than what is here.

Steam climbs and quietly forgets
the water it once was.
I pour, and let the evening be
exactly what it does.

items.title: Nihal Sarin enters the world top 20
items.body: The November FIDE list has Nihal Sarin at 2720, up 11 points and climbing from #30 to #19, a career-best ranking. It follows a 5/6 score and a board-two gold medal at the European Club Cup in Budva. At the top, Magnus Carlsen is on 2823, and Javokhir Sindarov sits at #4 with 2782.
items.q: What is Nihal Sarin's world ranking on the November 2026 FIDE list?
items.a: #19, rated 2720: his career best.

items.title: Southern Taurids peak this Thursday
items.body: The Southern Taurid meteor shower peaks in the early hours of 5 November. Expect a gentle 5 to 10 meteors an hour, but Taurids are slow and sometimes bright: the occasional fireball is their signature. The debris comes from Comet Encke. The Northern Taurids follow, peaking closer to 12 November, just after the 9 November new Moon gives a dark sky.
items.q: Which comet feeds the Taurid meteor showers?
items.a: Comet 2P/Encke.

items.title: OpenAI ships GPT-6.1 Terra for workflow agents
items.body: OpenAI rolled out GPT-6.1 Terra on 26 October, a mid-tier model aimed at computer use and workflow automation. It is available in ChatGPT Work, Codex and the API, and is priced at half of the GPT-5.6 Terra model it replaces. On OpenAI's own internal stress test, its error rate fell from 53.6% to 16.7% at low reasoning effort, and to 4.3% at maximum effort.
items.hook: Wonder: for your own agent tasks, would you rather pay for more 'thinking' per step, or for more steps?

items.title: Quick retrieval: this edition
items.body:
Close your eyes for 30 seconds and recall three things from today's feed without scrolling back. Then check.

Pulling memories out, rather than re-reading them, is how they stick.
items.q: Little's Law in one line?
items.a: Items in the system = arrival rate × time in system (L = λW).

items.body: There is nothing either good or bad, but thinking makes it so.

items.title: Older than the Aztecs
items.body: Teaching was happening at Oxford by 1096. The Aztec capital Tenochtitlan was founded in 1325, more than two centuries later.
items.hook: Which institutions around you will still exist in 900 years?

items.title: The first published program
items.body: In 1843 Ada Lovelace translated an article about Babbage's Analytical Engine and added notes three times longer than the original. Note G laid out step by step how the engine could compute Bernoulli numbers. It's often called the first published computer program, written for a machine that was never built.
items.hook: What would it feel like to write code for a machine that doesn't exist yet?

items.title: Park downhill
items.body:
Hemingway liked to stop writing while he still knew what came next, so the next morning's start was easy.

For ADHD this is gold. End every work block by writing one sentence: "Next, I will…". Starting is the hardest part; leave yourself a downhill start.
items.hook: What's the one-line 'next' for the task you'll open after this?

items.title: Two lamps
items.body:
Two lamps hung in a temple corridor. One burned bright and needed refilling twice a night. The other burned low and lasted till dawn.

The priest never compared them. He knew some hours need brightness and some need endurance, and a corridor needs both.

items.title: CAP, said properly
items.body:
CAP is often summarised as 'pick two of three.' More precisely: when a network partition happens, a distributed system must choose between consistency (refuse or delay answers) and availability (answer, possibly with stale data). When there's no partition, you can have both.

Brewer stated it in 2000; Gilbert and Lynch proved it in 2002.
items.q: When is CAP's trade-off forced?
items.a: Only during a network partition. Then you choose consistency or availability.

items.body: Learn thoroughly what is worth learning, then stand by it in how you live.

items.title: Aryabhata's spinning Earth
items.body: In 499 CE, at just 23, Aryabhata wrote the Aryabhatiya. He proposed that the stars' daily motion comes from Earth rotating on its axis, and gave a value of π accurate to four decimal places (3.1416). India's first satellite was named after him in 1975.
items.q: What did Aryabhata say explains the stars' daily motion?
items.a: Earth's rotation on its own axis.

items.title: Context isn't memory
items.body:
A model's context window is like a desk: whatever is on it right now, it can use. Memory is the filing cabinet: what you choose to pull back onto the desk later.

RAG (retrieval-augmented generation) is just a librarian who fetches the right files before each question. Most 'the AI forgot' problems are really retrieval problems.
items.hook: In your own systems, where is the right information sitting in a cabinet nobody opens?

items.title: Bananas are berries; strawberries aren't
items.body: Botanically, a berry develops from a single flower's ovary with seeds inside the flesh, so bananas, tomatoes and even brinjal qualify. A strawberry's 'seeds' are actually tiny fruits on the outside of a swollen stem base, so it isn't a true berry at all.

items.title: The Y2038 problem
items.body: Unix counts time as seconds since 1 January 1970. In a signed 32-bit integer, that counter overflows at 03:14:07 UTC on 19 January 2038 and wraps around to 1901. Most modern systems use 64 bits now, but old embedded devices and file formats may still break.
items.hook: What 32-bit assumptions are lurking in systems you've worked on?

items.title: Building a bridge (the Lucena position)
items.body:
Rook and pawn vs rook, your pawn on the 7th, your king on the queening square, enemy rook cutting your king off from the side. How do you get out and promote?

The classic method: bring your rook to the 4th rank, walk the king out, and when checks come, block with the rook. That's 'building a bridge.'
items.q: In the Lucena position, which rank does the rook go to, and why?
items.a: The 4th rank, counting from your side. That way it can step in front of your king to block the checks once the king leaves the pawn.

items.title: The inverted U
items.body:
In 1908 Yerkes and Dodson found that performance rises with arousal, but only up to a point. Then it falls. The peak sits lower for complex tasks than simple ones.

Translation: a little pressure sharpens you for routine work; for deep, tricky work (debugging, writing), calm wins.
items.hook: Is the stress you feel today helping simple tasks or hurting complex ones?

items.title: Late-November sky diary
items.body: Mark these: Nov 16, Mars passes close to Jupiter. Nov 24, the full Moon is a supermoon. Nov 25, Uranus reaches opposition, its closest and brightest of the year (still needs binoculars and a dark sky).

items.title: What the river knows
items.body:
It never argues with the stone.
It simply goes around,
and in a thousand years
the stone is sand,
and the river
is still a river.

items.title: Java 21 virtual threads, in one breath
items.body:
Platform threads map one-to-one onto OS threads and are expensive, so you pool them. Virtual threads (final in Java 21) are cheap threads managed by the JVM. When one blocks on I/O, the JVM parks it and frees the carrier thread.

Result: you can write simple blocking code and still handle a million concurrent requests.
items.q: What happens to a virtual thread when it blocks on I/O?
items.a: The JVM unmounts it from its carrier OS thread, which is freed to run another virtual thread.

items.title: Zero gets its rules
items.body: In 628 CE the mathematician Brahmagupta, in his Brahmasphutasiddhanta, wrote the first known rules for doing arithmetic with zero as a number in its own right: a number minus itself is zero, anything times zero is zero. He also wrestled with division by zero, a problem that still trips up our code.
items.q: Who first wrote down arithmetic rules for zero, and when?
items.a: Brahmagupta, in 628 CE.

items.body: Men are disturbed not by things, but by the principles and notions which they form concerning things.

items.title: Body doubling
items.body:
Some tasks get done simply because someone else is in the room. That's body doubling. The other person doesn't help; their presence just anchors your attention.

Works remotely too: a silent video call with a friend, or a 'focus room' online. Even saying "I'm starting X now" to someone counts.
items.hook: Who could be your silent co-worker for one hour this week?

items.title: The first programmers of ENIAC
items.body: ENIAC, unveiled in 1946, was programmed by six women: Kay McNulty, Betty Jennings, Betty Snyder, Marlyn Wescoff, Fran Bilas and Ruth Lichterman. There were no programming languages; they worked from wiring diagrams and plugged cables by hand. For decades they went largely uncredited.

items.title: Three hearts, blue blood
items.body: An octopus has three hearts: two pump blood through the gills, one pumps it around the body. Its blood is blue because it carries oxygen with copper-based haemocyanin instead of our iron-based haemoglobin.
items.hook: Why would copper beat iron in cold, low-oxygen seawater?

items.title: The Zeigarnik effect, honestly
items.body:
In the 1920s Bluma Zeigarnik noticed that waiters remembered unpaid orders perfectly and forgot them once paid. Her experiments suggested unfinished tasks stay mentally 'open.'

Later replications are mixed, but one useful finding holds: writing down a concrete plan for an unfinished task quiets the mental nagging. Closing the loop on paper is enough.
items.hook: What open loop is humming in your head right now? Write the next step down.

items.title: A teaspoon of neutron star
items.body: A neutron star packs more mass than the Sun into a ball about 20 km wide, roughly the size of a city. A teaspoon of its material would weigh on the order of a billion tonnes on Earth.
items.q: Roughly how wide is a neutron star?
items.a: About 20 km, city-sized, while holding more mass than the Sun.

items.title: More games than atoms
items.body: Claude Shannon estimated the number of possible chess games at about 10^120, now called the Shannon number. The observable universe has roughly 10^80 atoms. No computer will ever solve chess by brute force, which is why intuition and pattern still matter.
items.hook: If brute force is impossible, how do engines play so well?

items.title: Evals are the unit tests of AI
items.body:
You wouldn't ship code without tests, but people ship prompts without evals all the time. An eval is a fixed set of inputs with known good outputs that you re-run after every change.

Start tiny: 10 real examples, a pass/fail column. It turns 'feels better' into 'is better.'

items.title: The three-beat story
items.body:
Every story that holds a room has three beats: someone wants something → something gets in the way → they (or we) change.

No change, no story; just an event. Before your next speech or blog post, write one line: "Who changed, and how?"
items.hook: What's the smallest true story from your week that has all three beats?

items.title: Idempotency keys: making 'retry' safe
items.body:
A payment request times out. Did it go through? If the client retries, you might charge twice.

The fix: the client sends a unique idempotency key with the request. The server stores the result against that key, so a repeat with the same key returns the stored result instead of doing the work again. Stripe made the pattern famous; every order and payment API needs it.
items.q: What does the server do when it sees an idempotency key it has seen before?
items.a: Returns the stored response from the first attempt without re-executing the operation.

items.title: The temple whose shadow stories are wrong
items.body: Rajaraja Chola I completed the Brihadeeswarar temple at Thanjavur around 1010 CE. Its tower rises about 66 metres. A popular legend says the tower casts no shadow at noon. It does cast one; it just falls on its own broad base. The real wonder is that it has stood for over a thousand years.
items.hook: Why do we love myths about things that are already remarkable?

items.body: There are more things, Lucilius, likely to frighten us than there are to crush us; we suffer more often in imagination than in reality.

items.title: Make time visible
items.body: Time blindness is real: an ADHD brain often feels only 'now' and 'not now.' Move time outside your head. Use a visual countdown timer on the desk, or say out loud "this gets 25 minutes." Analog clocks help more than digital ones, because you can see how much of the hour is left.
items.hook: Where in your day does time disappear the most?

items.title: Java was almost called Oak
items.body: In 1991 James Gosling's team at Sun started the 'Green Project' to program consumer devices. Their language was called Oak, after a tree outside his office. A trademark clash forced a new name, and in 1995 it shipped as Java, sold on 'write once, run anywhere.'
items.q: What was Java's original name, and why did it change?
items.a: Oak. The name was already trademarked, so it was renamed Java before the 1995 launch.

items.title: Cleopatra and the Moon landing
items.body: Cleopatra lived closer in time to the Apollo 11 Moon landing than to the building of the Great Pyramid of Giza. The pyramid went up around 2560 BCE; she died in 30 BCE. That's about 2,530 years before her and 1,999 years after.
items.hook: What else feels ancient but is actually 'recent'?

items.title: The physiological sigh
items.body:
Two inhales through the nose (a full one, then a short top-up) and one long, slow exhale through the mouth. A 2023 Stanford study found that five minutes a day of this 'cyclic sighing' lifted mood more than the same time spent on mindfulness meditation.

It's the fastest manual brake on stress your body offers.

source.name: Balban et al., Cell Reports Medicine (2023)

items.title: Capablanca's unusual advice: learn endings first
items.body: José Raúl Capablanca, world champion 1921–27, told beginners to study the endgame before anything else. With few pieces on the board, you learn what each piece is actually worth. Openings are memory. Endgames are understanding.
items.hook: What's the 'endgame' of your own field: the simplest situation where the fundamentals show clearly?

items.title: Leonids peak Nov 17–18
items.body: The Leonid meteor shower peaks on the night of 17–18 November, at around 15 meteors an hour under dark skies. The Moon will have set by the second half of the night. Leonids are among the fastest meteors, hitting the air at about 70 km/s. They're dust from Comet Tempel–Tuttle.
items.hook: A grain of sand making a streak across the whole sky. How much energy is that?

items.title: Java: when a HashMap bucket turns into a tree
items.body: Since Java 8, if one HashMap bucket collects more than 8 entries (and the table has at least 64 slots), that bucket turns from a linked list into a red-black tree. Worst-case lookup drops from O(n) to O(log n). It's a defence against bad hashCode() methods and hash-flooding attacks.
items.q: Two conditions trigger treeification. What are they?
items.a: More than 8 entries in one bucket (TREEIFY_THRESHOLD) and a table capacity of at least 64. Below 64 slots, HashMap resizes instead.

items.title: The clockmaker's apprentice
items.body:
The apprentice asked why the old man oiled clocks that were running perfectly.

"Because," he said, "the day it stops, you'll be busy with a hundred others. A clock doesn't ask for care when it needs it. It asks a month later, all at once."

The boy thought this was about clocks. Thirty years later, oiling a quiet clock in his own shop, he realised it never had been.

items.title: An agent is just a loop
items.body:
Strip the hype and every AI agent is: observe → decide → act → check → repeat.

Most agent failures aren't bad thinking. They're a bad 'check' step: the agent never verifies its action worked, so errors compound silently. If you build agents, spend your effort on the check.
items.hook: In your own work, where is the 'check' step weakest?

items.title: A day on Venus outlasts its year
items.body: Venus turns on its axis once every 243 Earth days but goes around the Sun in about 225. It also spins backwards compared with most planets, so on Venus the Sun would rise in the west.
items.hook: What could have knocked a whole planet into spinning backwards?

items.title: Forgetting is the point
items.body:
In 1885 Hermann Ebbinghaus memorised nonsense syllables and tracked how fast he lost them. Recall fell steeply within the first day, then flattened.

The twist: each time you pull a memory back just as it's fading, it decays more slowly afterwards. That's the spacing effect. Struggling a little to remember is the signal that learning is happening.
items.q: When is the best time to review something?
items.a: Just as you're about to forget it, so retrieval takes some effort. Then space the next review further out.

items.title: The first actual bug
items.body: On 9 September 1947, operators of the Harvard Mark II found a moth trapped in a relay. They taped it into the logbook with the note "First actual case of bug being found." Grace Hopper loved telling the story. Engineers had already been using "bug" for faults, so the joke was that this one was literal.
items.q: What machine was the famous moth found in?
items.a: The Harvard Mark II, in 1947.

items.body: Your right is to the work alone, never to its fruits.
items.hook: What would today look like if you judged it only by effort given?

items.title: A dam that has worked for nearly 2,000 years
items.body: The Kallanai, or Grand Anicut, on the Kaveri is credited to the Chola king Karikalan, around the 2nd century CE. It's among the oldest water-diversion structures in the world still in use, and it still feeds irrigation channels in the delta today.
items.hook: What makes a structure last 2,000 years when most concrete gives out in 100?

items.title: Interest is your ignition, not importance
items.body:
Many ADHD coaches describe attention as running on interest rather than importance. The usual starters go by the acronym INCUP: Interest, Novelty, Challenge, Urgency, Passion.

When a task won't start, don't ask "why can't I make myself?" Ask which of the five you can add. Make it a race against a timer (challenge, urgency), try a new tool (novelty), or attach it to a question you care about (interest).
items.hook: Which of the five is cheapest to add to your next boring task?

items.title: Gukesh vs Sindarov: the world title match is three weeks away
items.body: The 2026 World Championship match runs in Geneva from November 25 to December 15, with reigning champion Gukesh D defending against Javokhir Sindarov of Uzbekistan. Both players are about 20, making it the youngest pairing ever to contest the title.
items.hook: What changes in a 14-game match that doesn't exist in a tournament?

items.title: Cab window, 10 pm
items.body:
The city folds its noise away
like laundry into drawers.
One lit window, then another —
someone else's evening, not yours,
and somehow that is restful:
to pass a hundred lives
and owe none of them a reply.

items.title: Little's Law: the formula hiding inside every queue
items.body:
L = λ × W. Items in the system = arrival rate × average time each one stays.

If 10 incidents arrive a day and each takes 3 days to close, you'll average about 30 open. The law doesn't care who works harder. To shrink the queue you can only reduce arrivals or reduce time-in-system.
items.hook: Which lever is easier in your queue: fewer arrivals, or less time per item?
items.q: Arrival rate doubles, time-per-item stays the same. What happens to the open queue?
items.a: It doubles. L = λW is linear in both.

items.title: Mistral opens up a trillion-parameter model
items.body: Mistral released Large 4 with open weights: a trillion-parameter multimodal model that organisations can run on their own servers. It's pitched at software development and defensive security work, where companies don't want sensitive data leaving their walls.

items.title: Before dawn: the Moon visits Mars and Jupiter
items.body: Over the next couple of mornings a thin waning Moon slides past Mars and Jupiter, then Regulus, the heart of Leo. Look east in the hour before sunrise. Jupiter is the steady bright one; Mars is fainter and faintly orange.
items.q: Why do stars twinkle but planets mostly don't?
items.a: Stars are so far away they're effectively single points, so air turbulence bends that one point around. A planet shows a tiny disc, and the wobbles from different parts of the disc average out.
